ai-2c43c28405.headline: Anthropic officially files for its public debut
ai-2c43c28405.fulltext:
After weeks of leaked S-1s, Anthropic finally filed for an initial public offering on Monday, setting the stage for one of the most closely watched public debuts in modern U.S. history.
Anthropic, which plans to list under the ticker “ANT,” recorded revenue of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year, according to the firm’s latest SEC filing.
That revenue came off the back of an operating loss of $693 million, an improvement from the $2.1 billion in operating losses that Anthropic recorded in the first half of 2025. Anthropic’s net loss, however, hit $80.7 billion, which was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt. The company says it “may not achieve or sustain profitability in the future.”
The filing also provided more color on the scale of Anthropic’s enterprise business. As of the end of September, Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending $100,000 or more annually; 1,900 customers spending $1 million or more; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more.
As previously reported, Anthropic’s governance structure will enable Anthropic’s seven co-founders to maintain control once the company goes public. Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah will make up the “Founder LLC,” which will collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power — a move Anthropic says is designed to preserve the company’s AI safety mission, per the filing.
Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, established in 2023 to ensure the company pursues its public benefit mission, will have the authority to appoint most of the company’s board.
The governance structure is controversial because it means voting power is not proportional to the founders’ economic ownership, and therefore public shareholders will have little practical control over a company building technology that, by its own admission, poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it hopes to raise nor its proposed share price.

ai-6f8e3f33bb.headline: Broadcom Arranges $63 Billion Deal to Finance Anthropic’s Chips
ai-6f8e3f33bb.fulltext:
[Text below is CNA's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Chipmaker Broadcom Inc. has arranged a $63 billion deal with Bank of America Corp., Blackstone Inc., Citigroup Inc. and Morgan Stanley to finance the purchase of chips for AI model developer Anthropic PBC.
The deal is being done through a new special purpose vehicle with committed financing from the financial firms to buy Broadcom chips and lease them to Anthropic, the firms said in a joint statement on Monday. Broadcom is backstopping a portion of the financing with what’s known as residual value support.
Wall Street banks, Blackstone line up $63 billion to finance Broadcom AI chips for Anthropic
Oct 26 : Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley will provide $63 billion in financing to buy Broadcom's AI chips and networking gear for Anthropic, in one of the largest debt deals tied to the AI buildout.
Broadcom is providing "residual value support" to lenders, who are providing first lien loans or senior debt, effectively providing a significant guarantee in the financing structure.
The latest deal highlights the growing role of banks and alternative asset managers in financing the infrastructure needed to support rising demand for AI computing capacity.
Anthropic filed for a potentially record-breaking IPO on Monday, even as disclosures of steep losses and security concerns threatened to test investor appetite for the AI heavyweight.
The size of the first lien loans or senior debt is about $43.5 billion, according to two sources familiar with the matter, or 69 per cent of total financing.
Blackstone will provide the committed portion of the second-lien financing - which ranks below senior debt - while Bank of America, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley are arranging the first-lien financing, the statement said.
Chipmakers have provided guarantees in the past to absorb potential declines in the value of the assets, such as advanced chips and data infrastructure.
The release did not disclose the breakdown of the loans, while Broadcom did not respond to a request for comment.
Rising AI demand is driving massive investment in computing infrastructure as technology companies race to secure capacity for increasingly complex workloads.
The transaction will be carried out through a newly formed special purpose vehicle that will purchase Broadcom's AI accelerators and networking equipment and lease them to the Claude maker, the companies said on Monday.
Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley are arranging the first-lien financing.
Deliveries are expected to begin in 2027 as part of a previously announced strategic compute capacity agreement involving Broadcom, the companies said.
Apollo and Blackstone had agreed to finance a $35 billion expansion of Anthropic's AI computing capacity under a prior agreement with Broadcom. Broadcom's backstop in that deal was up to $29 billion, it said in a filing.
While Moody's described Broadcom as one of the strongest large technology companies, it warned that the risk would increase if multiple transactions were undertaken over a short period to meet the sizable funding needs of frontier AI labs.

india-deep-tech-09a5d8e245.headline: India's VC Funding Remains Flat, Focus Shifts to Deeptech
india-deep-tech-09a5d8e245.fulltext:
India's venture capital funding for startups has seen a period of stagnation over the last three years, even as a significant shift towards larger, concentrated investments in deeptech and AI sectors signals evolving investor strategies.
Key Points
- India's VC equity funding for startups has remained largely flat over the past three years, with $10.9 billion raised across 1,253 rounds in 2026 (January-October 15).
- Despite flat overall funding, the average equity funding per round increased to $8.6 million in 2026, up from $5.1 million in 2025, indicating a greater concentration of capital in fewer startups.
- VCs are increasingly favouring deeptech, AI, and clean energy startups, with a significant portion of investment going to a select group of companies like Sarvam AI, Inox Clean Energy, and Emergent BioSolutions.
- The top 10 startups by funds raised accounted for nearly 36 per cent of all VC equity funding during the period, securing a combined $3.92 billion.
- The stagnation in VC investment is attributed to cautious investors, subdued stock markets, and the longer investment horizon required for deeptech companies.
India’s venture capital (VC) equity funding for startups has remained largely flat over the past three years. Between January and October 15, funding in calendar year 2026 added up to $10.9 billion across 1,253 rounds, up just 6.8 per cent from the same period a year earlier.
In the corresponding period of 2025, startups raised $10.2 billion in equity funding through 1,982 rounds, compared with $10.4 billion across the first 10 months of 2024.
Shifting Investment Landscape
According to Tracxn data, the average equity funding per round rose to $8.6 million in 2026, from $5.1 million in the year-ago period. The higher average, despite the sharp decline in the number of rounds, points to a greater concentration of capital in fewer startups.
VCs have increasingly favoured a select group of startups, with a large share of investment concentrated in a handful of companies.
Several of the top 10 startups by funds raised, including generative artificial intelligence (AI) startup Sarvam AI, clean energy developer Inox Clean Energy, and life sciences company Emergent BioSolutions, secured funding in two separate rounds during the period.
Sarvam, for instance, raised $255.1 million in a Series B round in January, followed by another $90.4 million in August.
The top 10 startups by total funds raised between January and October accounted for nearly 36 per cent of all VC equity funding during the period, securing a combined $3.92 billion.
Valuations also rose. Among the top 10 startups, publicly available data for seven showed their combined valuations climbing to $10.3 billion in 2026, from $9.3 billion in 2025.
Reasons for Stagnation and Future Outlook
Explaining the near-stagnation in VC investment, Anjan Ray, investment partner at Navam Capital, which invests in deeptech companies, said, "We hypothesise that VC funding has been relatively flat because their sources of funds — namely family offices, financial institutions, and high networth individuals who have invested in the stock market — are staying out as the market remains subdued.
"Also, less VC money is going towards consumertech and finance startups, and more towards deeptech, where one needs a longer horizon, perhaps as much as a decade, before an exit. Investors are therefore proceeding cautiously as they learn about deeptech, its ecosystem, and the potential risks and disruptions."
The largest deal during the period was undertaken by Nxtra Data, the data centre business of Bharti Airtel.
It raised $1 billion in a round led by Alpha Wave Global.
Mumbai-based Neysa, which helps companies integrate AI into their operations, raised $600 million in a Series B round led by Blackstone.
The funding lifted its valuation from $800 million to $1.4 billion.
Sarvam, one of the companies supported by the IndiaAI Mission, raised a total of $345 million across two rounds from prominent investors, including Nvidia Corporation and HCLTech.
The funding helped it attain unicorn status in June, with a valuation of $1.5 billion.

india-1200ddf73b.headline: Face-Offs at India-China Border Are Continuing at Multiple Points, ITBP Chief Confirms - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
india-1200ddf73b.source: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
india-1200ddf73b.fulltext:
Claims by civil society groups and media in India’s northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh that Chinese troops have been crossing into Indian territory, which the Narendra Modi government has repeatedly denied, were confirmed by a top Indian official last week.
At an event in Alwar, Rajasthan, on October 22, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur said that face-offs are happening between Indian and Chinese forces “at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues.”
Kapur’s remarks on Thursday about the face-offs are hardly a revelation. Civil society groups and media in the northeast Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, which borders China, have been drawing attention to the fragile, even alarming situation along the frontier since June-July.
In a letter dated June 26, 2026, to the deputy commissioner of Upper Subansiri, the Nah Welfare Society (NWS) said that the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) had occupied Indian territory in and around Taksing, including Oying in the Asaphila area, Paniar in the Chujarta area, Marpan in Marnafe, Portrang Lake, and Tingdingtang. In addition to establishing a military camp in the area, the PLA has also built roads, bridges, and military camps in several locations traditionally used by local communities for grazing, hunting, and collecting forest produce. A Taksing-based tribal organization, the NWS expressed “deep grief” over the PLA’s gradual occupation of ancestral lands, which it said, has intensified since 2020.
Soon after the contents of the NWS’ memorandum became public, the Indian Army categorically dismissed the “reports” as “incorrect and without any basis.” Then came videos claiming the PLA had advanced 50-60 km into Indian territory. The Indian government’s Press Information Bureau Fact Check unit dismissed the reports as ” fake;” the videos did not pertain to the India-China border, it said. This was followed by reports and videos of “skirmishes” in the Taksing Circle on July 25-26. The “confrontation” reportedly “continued for nearly a week before the situation was brought under control following intervention by senior commanders from both sides.” However, Arunachal Pradesh’s Home Minister Mama Natung dismissed the reports of Chinese encroachment as “just rumors.”
Now, for the first time, there is official confirmation of confrontations at multiple locations along the India-China border in Arunachal Pradesh. And this confirmation has come from the head of the ITBP, the force that guards the India-China border.
The entire India-China border is disputed. The two countries not only have differing perceptions of where the Line of Actual Control, the de facto border, runs, but they also claim swathes of territory under the other’s control. China claims 90,000 sq km of territory that roughly coincides with Arunachal Pradesh. India claims 38,000 sq km of territory in Aksai Chin that China occupied during the 1962 border war, and another 5,300 sq km in the Shaksgam Valley of Jammu and Kashmir that Pakistan occupied in 1947-48 and gifted to China in 1963.
Besides the war in 1962, which China won, the two sides have engaged in skirmishes and standoffs several times over the decades, including at Samdurong Chu in Arunachal in 1986-87, at the Doklam trijunction of China, India and Bhutan in 2017, and at Galwan in Ladakh in June 2020, which resulted in the death of 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers.
Interestingly, China’s interest in Arunachal Pradesh has waxed and waned over time. After occupying Arunachal, then known as the North East Frontier Agency, for several weeks during the 1962 war, the PLA pulled out. Indeed, it did not seem interested in pressing any claims here, and under a swap proposal, was willing to give up claims in the eastern sector, in return for India accepting its control over Aksai Chin in the western sector.
It was only from the mid-1980s that China began reasserting claims over what it calls “Zangnan” or “South Tibet,” at bilateral talks, through military intrusions, by pushing back Indian patrol teams, objecting to visits of Indian leaders to Arunachal Pradesh, refusing to issue visas to Indian passport holders from the state on the argument that they are not Indian, and announcing “standardized” or Chinese names for places and geographical features in the state. According to a 2025 Pentagon report, Arunachal Pradesh is among China’s “core interests.”
In recent months, India and China have engaged in a slew of talks. On August 6, the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs was held in New Delhi. Then on August 26, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval met with China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi at the 25th round of Special Representatives’ talks on the Boundary Question in Beijing. On September 6, the Indian Army and the PLA held their first Corps Commander-level meeting in the Eastern Sector at the Vacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting Point in Arunachal Pradesh.
India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping shook hands and chatted at the SCO Summit at Bishkek on August 31, and held a meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in Delhi on September 12.
If the India-China face-offs are continuing, as the ITBP Director General Kapur said they are, it is clear the talks have had little impact in deterring the PLA.
One obvious reason is that Prime Minister Modi’s China strategy is guided more by his interest in beefing up his image among his supporters than taking a strong position against China. His government has repeatedly denied PLA encroachment into Indian controlled territory. “Neither is anyone inside our territory nor is any of our post captured,” Modi grandly declared at an all-party meeting days after the Galwan clashes. The recent spate of denials by the government over PLA’s encroachments in Arunachal is part of the same short-sighted vision. It has weakened India’s hand at talks.
Even more baffling is the Modi government’s withdrawal of ITBP companies from the border. Since June-July, massive anti-government protests in the capital have rattled the Modi government. In response, it has pulled out ITBP personnel from the India-China border and redeployed them in Delhi at a time when the border situation is volatile. Clearly, using the ITBP to crush unarmed civilian protestors in Delhi is more important to Modi than using the force to push back PLA advances at the Arunachal border.
Under the BJP government, almost every Indian state/union territory bordering China is roiled in unrest. Arunachal’s civil society has strongly opposed a mega dam being constructed in the state’s Upper Siang district. The state’s inept handling of public concerns raised over displacement, environmental impact, and loss of livelihoods, and its use of force to deal with protests have resulted in the escalation of the conflict. On October 23, Upper Siang witnessed unprecedented scenes of violence.
Already, Arunachalis are upset with the government for not acting on their apprehensions over PLA encroachment into their traditional lands and hunting grounds. Delhi’s use of the iron fist now to put down their protests will fuel further anger. This will only add to India’s troubles in a sensitive border region.

work-careers-64bfe6abbd.headline: Microsoft offers voluntary exit package to 60K employees across India, US, UK and Canada
work-careers-64bfe6abbd.fulltext:
Business
Microsoft offers voluntary exit package to 60K employees across India, US, UK and Canada
Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India, but the number eligible for the voluntary exit offer is unclear. Eligible staff have until December 1 to decide.
Tech giant Microsoft on Monday announced a voluntary exit programme for eligible employees in India, the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, offering financial support and career planning resources to those who choose to leave the company, according to a blog post by the firm.
Microsoft has about 23,000 employees in India, although it is not immediately clear how many would be eligible for the programme. Globally, around 60,000 employees are eligible.
Eligible employees in India will have until December 1 to decide whether to accept the voluntary exit offer, it is learnt.
The package is understood to be similar to a standard severance arrangement, including one month's base salary for every completed year of service, along with health insurance and career transition services.
Microsoft Executive Vice President and Chief People Officer Amy Coleman said in her blog post that the voluntary exit offer (VEO) would be available to employees at level 70 and below in participating teams across the four countries. The internal job grades span various levels of seniority at Microsoft.
The time-limited initiative aims to provide greater flexibility to employees considering opportunities outside the company, she wrote.
Meanwhile, a Microsoft spokesperson said the company continued to invest in India's talent and technology ecosystem and was supporting the country's AI ambitions with $20.5 billion in committed investment between 2025 and 2029 across cloud and AI infrastructure, skilling and operations.
"We are also on track to fulfil our commitment of equipping 20 million people across India with AI skills by 2030," the spokesperson said.
Coleman said the programme would give employees the option to make the transition with support while allowing participating businesses to adjust their workforces in response to evolving requirements.
"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organisations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs," Coleman said.
The company clarified that the programme would not be implemented uniformly across its operations, with participation depending on individual business priorities, customer commitments and workforce requirements.
Eligible employees will receive emails detailing the terms of their voluntary exit offers, the blog post said.
"The Voluntary Exit Offer is new for us. We'll learn from it," Coleman said.
She added that Microsoft would continue helping employees develop new skills and explore internal career opportunities, where appropriate.
"There is no one-size-fits-all approach for every team or every employee," Coleman said, emphasising that the company would seek to balance changing business requirements with opportunities for employees to grow and contribute.
(With inputs from PTI)

india-6bd8b4f867.headline: India, US fine-tuning trade deal after concluding most discussions, says minister Piyush Goyal
india-6bd8b4f867.fulltext:
Utpal BhaskarPublished26 Oct 2026, 09:45 PM IST
THE HAGUE: India and the US have concluded most discussions on a proposed trade agreement and are fine-tuning the deal, commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday, signalling progress towards an agreement that could bring greater certainty to Indian exporters facing shifting US tariff policies.
“In the last four and a half years, friends, we have entered into nine free trade agreements or bilateral trade agreements. I'm adding the US in that, we have concluded most of the discussions and are fine-tuning the agreement,” Goyal said at the India-Netherlands Business Forum in The Hague.
For Indian exporters, a deal could provide greater predictability in pricing US-bound shipments and negotiating contracts. Any boost to exports would also offer timely support to an economy grappling with the fallout from the wars in West Asia and Ukraine.
Goyal’s remarks follow a recent visit to India by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the two countries were “very, very close” to a trade agreement, with a small number of issues remaining to be resolved.
“We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without (inaudible) agreement. I think there’s a small number of items to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly,” Rubio had said.
Goyal said India’s expanding network of trade agreements, including those under negotiation, would give it preferential access to economies accounting for $85 trillion of the $115 trillion global GDP.
“Just to give you the context of India thinking on opening our doors. Until 2014, all the free trade agreements put together opened a GDP of $10 trillion where we had preferential access or where we opened our doors to those countries,” said Goyal, who is on an official visit to the Netherlands.
“India would have opened its doors and had preferential market access to an additional $60 trillion worth of economies around the globe. Together, now we have $70 trillion of economies where we would have preferential trade agreements. I have eight more negotiations which are underway right now which will add another $15 trillion. So India would be opening its doors to $85 trillion out of $115 trillion. That's around 76% of global GDP with which we are building our partnership, opening the doors on a complementary and cooperative nature to greater business engagement,” Goyal said.
Bilateral trade between India and the US rose 6.53% to $140.76 billion in fiscal year 2026 (FY26), from $132.2 billion in the previous year. India’s trade surplus narrowed to $33.9 billion from $40.9 billion. Exports to the US edged up to $87.31 billion from $86.51 billion, while imports rose 17.16% to $53.45 billion from $45.62 billion.
The proposed agreement comes as global supply chains face disruption from the wars in West Asia and Ukraine, alongside a broader global slowdown. Goods exports remain important to India’s growth, with provisional commerce ministry data showing merchandise exports rose 23% year-on-year to $44.4 billion in September. Imports increased 8% to $74.61 billion, narrowing the trade deficit to $30.21 billion from $33 billion a year earlier.
Goyal said India remained on track for strong growth despite international uncertainties.
“Despite all the problems of the world, we are the fastest growing large economy. We grew 7.7% last year. The IMF (International Monetary Fund) just came out with numbers…We're expected to go upward of 7%. My own guess is we'll grow 7.5% this year,” he said.
The IMF has raised its growth forecast for India by 60 basis points to 7% for FY27, reinforcing its position as the fastest-growing major economy.
Ramita Mishra contributed to the story.
The writer is in The Hague as the guest of Confederation of Indian Industry.

deep-tech-a9e4c1df42.headline: Intel to acquire Israeli quantum startup Classiq for $2.3 billion
deep-tech-a9e4c1df42.fulltext:
Intel to acquire Israeli quantum startup Classiq for $2.3 billion
The deal marks a record acquisition in the quantum computing industry and a major exit for Israel’s tech sector, with Classiq’s founders, employees and early investors poised for substantial returns.
The first major exit for Israel’s quantum industry: Classiq, a developer of operating systems for quantum computers, is being acquired by Intel for $2.3 billion in a combination of cash and stock. The deal would make Classiq the most expensive quantum company acquisition to date, by a significant margin. The previous record was set last year, when IonQ acquired Oxford Ionics for $1 billion.
The transaction also marks a major acquisition for Intel, which paid approximately $1 billion for Israeli mobility company Moovit six years ago and $2 billion for Habana Labs a year earlier. Intel has made other acquisitions since then, including the Israeli company Granulate, but those deals were valued in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Intel has not acquired another Israeli company since the Granulate deal in 2022.
For Israelis accustomed to multibillion-dollar exits in cybersecurity, $2.3 billion might not seem particularly large. In quantum computing, however, it represents a landmark deal. Despite the excitement surrounding the field, quantum computers have yet to achieve widespread practical commercial use. There are currently only 117 quantum computers worldwide, and they remain prohibitively expensive and largely inaccessible.
Quantum computing has shown promise for decades, and the field has recorded several significant breakthroughs over the past two years. Yet it has not experienced its own “ChatGPT moment,” a breakthrough that would bring the technology into widespread use.
Despite its small size, Israel is considered one of the world’s five leading countries in quantum computing, both in the number of companies operating in the field and in the volume of private investment. Intel’s acquisition of Classiq for more than $2 billion could draw greater investor attention to Israel and provide another catalyst for the development of its quantum industry.
The deal recalls Intel’s acquisition of Mobileye, the autonomous-driving company founded by Amnon Shashua, a decade ago. That transaction helped trigger a wave of investment in Israeli companies in the sector. The hope is that Classiq’s exit will have a similar effect, with even better long-term results for the industry.
For Classiq’s founders, employees and investors, the acquisition represents an impressive exit for a company founded just six years ago. Classiq currently employs around 150 people. Employees collectively hold 10% of the company’s shares, equivalent to $230 million at the acquisition price, although the proceeds will vary among individuals. Intel has also allocated more than $100 million in retention grants to encourage employees to remain with the company.
Classiq was founded by Nir Minerbi, Amir Naveh and his father, Prof. Yehuda Naveh. Minerbi is the CEO, Amir Naveh is the CPO, and Yehuda Naveh is the CTO. Minerbi and the younger Naveh are graduates of the Israel Defense Forces’ Talpiot program, as are many of the company’s employees. Yehuda Naveh previously held a senior position at IBM’s Israeli development center. Each of the three founders is expected to receive between $80 million and $100 million from the deal.
Classiq generates revenue, but its annual revenue remains in the tens of millions of dollars, well below an annual run rate of $100 million. The acquisition price therefore represents a substantial valuation multiple for a relatively young company.
Classiq occupies a distinctive position in the quantum computing industry. It develops software that serves as an operating system for quantum computers, bridging the gap between complex hardware and the people and organizations seeking to use it. The company’s ambition is to become the “Windows” of quantum computing.
IBM, a pioneer in quantum computing, is its main competitor. Estimates suggest that Classiq has already surpassed IBM in market share, although the companies’ positions depend on how that market is measured. Classiq’s software is hardware-agnostic, meaning it is designed to work across different quantum computing platforms rather than being tied to a single manufacturer.
Its customers span several industries, including banking, automotive and pharmaceuticals. They include BMW, Rolls-Royce, HSBC, Deloitte, Toshiba and Citi.
Classiq has raised approximately $200 million to date, making the acquisition a profitable outcome for its investors as well. Its most recent funding round, a $110 million raise in 2025, valued the company at an estimated $600 million to $700 million, far below the acquisition price.
Entrée Capital, which led Classiq’s pre-seed round and is its largest shareholder, stands to gain the most. The fund is expected to receive more than $300 million on an investment of just a few million dollars. Team8 Capital, the company’s second-largest shareholder, holds a 9% stake.
The deal is also expected to benefit Israeli savers through The Phoenix, which holds a 7.5% stake in Classiq. Unlike many recent Israeli technology exits, most of which have involved cybersecurity companies, Classiq is incorporated in Israel. The state is therefore expected to collect tax revenue from the transaction beyond the taxes paid by founders and employees who sell their shares.
However, because a significant portion of the consideration is in Intel stock, not all the proceeds will be realized immediately in cash.
One of Classiq’s private investors is Lip-Bu Tan, Intel’s current CEO, who has led the chipmaker’s turnaround over the past year and a half. Tan invested in Classiq personally before becoming CEO of the company now acquiring the startup. According to sources close to Classiq, he recused himself from discussions concerning the acquisition.
Other notable investors include NightDragon, a fund led by Dave DeWalt, who previously headed cybersecurity company McAfee.
Until recently, Classiq had been exploring a potential IPO on Wall Street, where several quantum computing companies have gone public over the past year. Most entered the public markets through mergers with special-purpose acquisition companies, or SPACs, and their subsequent share-price performance has been weak in recent months.
The only company to go public through a traditional IPO was Quantinuum, which debuted at a peak valuation of $15 billion. It has since lost 35% of its value and is currently valued at approximately $9.5 billion. IonQ, which went public through a SPAC merger in 2021, is now the most highly valued publicly traded quantum company, with a market capitalization of around $13 billion.
At $2.3 billion, the Classiq acquisition would place the Israeli company among the five most highly valued businesses in the global quantum computing sector. The valuation also illustrates the premium Intel is willing to pay for a company operating in a field that has yet to reach broad commercial adoption.
Like many founders, Minerbi and Naveh had spoken of global expansion and building an independent company. But with Intel offering $2.3 billion for a business that had raised approximately $200 million and was valued at $600 million to $700 million in its latest funding round, the acquisition represents a substantial outcome for its shareholders and a major milestone for Israel’s quantum industry.

global-economics-4426e4ff37.headline: EXCLUSIVE: Ambani, Adani outlets among Indian publishers contesting Modi’s privacy law
global-economics-4426e4ff37.fulltext:
[Text below is The Hindu's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
The Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which has members drawn from across the media spectrum, including those owned by the Ambani and Adani Groups, have challenged the Union government’s privacy law as a violation of journalistic freedom.
A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant is scheduled to hear a batch of petitions filed by activists on October 27.
Also read | Supreme Court to examine impact of data protection law on RTI, investigative journalism
The petition filed by the DNPA, which is also listed before the Bench, challenged specific provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025.
The DNPA said the law was completely in contravention with the law laid down by the Supreme Court in its privacy judgment, which held the right inviolable and fundamental to human dignity and life.
“They impermissibly restrict the fundamental right to information and freedom of speech and expression,” the petition said.
The law fails “to provide any exemption in favour of journalistic activity as a distinct class of processing, entitled to constitutional protection under Article 14 and 19(l)(a) of the Constitution of India and threatens the full spectrum of Journalistic activity carried out by journalists, ground reporters, citizens, whistleblowers, RTI activists, and other stakeholders, and strikes at the core of our democratic framework and runs contrary to the basic tenets of the Constitution of India,” the petition said.
It said publishers, editors, reporters and correspondents were, as a consequence of the law, brought within a regime of notice and prior consent, compelled erasure, and verifiable consent.
Section 36 of the DPDP Act, read with Rule 23 and the Seventh Schedule of the DPDP Rules, vested the Central government with an unbridled and standardless authority to requisition any information from any data fiduciary or intermediary, unaccompanied by judicial oversight, any requirement of necessity or proportionality, or notice to the affected data principal.
“Such a power is capable of being turned to the identification and targeting of journalistic sources and is thus constitutionally infirm,” the petition said.
Section 44 (3) of the DPDP Act, by amending Section 8 (1 )(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005, has placed every category of “personal information” beyond the reach of disclosure.
Further, by amending the Right to Information Act 2005, the DPDP Act has created an absolute bar on the seeking of information relating to public offices.

ai-4baf7ea00d.headline: Meta plans $95bn stock offering to help cover AI expansion
ai-4baf7ea00d.fulltext:
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta has announced plans for $95bn (£71bn) of fundraising to cover its AI expenditure, even as Elon Musk warned that funding for smaller players in the sector was drying up.
The owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp is a leading investor in AI and is ploughing multibillion-dollar sums into datacentres, the central nervous systems of the technology.
Meta’s announcement on Monday came after Musk added to the pressure on “neocloud” datacentre providers – which lease computing power to AI companies – by saying the sector faced “death and consolidation” amid concerns over the sustainability of their funding.
The Meta fundraising will come in two parts. In the first, the company plans to raise $35bn through new “underwritten public offerings” – a sale of company stock. This has some big-name backers, with chipmakers Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom all showing interest, Meta said. These “cornerstone investors” could buy up to $5bn of the stock on offer.
In the second, Meta also plans to launch a $60bn “at-the-market offering” to sell new common stock to investors at the going market rate in future. That offering involves selling Meta’s new class C stock, which it announced it was creating last week. These class C shares do not have voting rights, so can be sold without diluting Zuckerberg’s control of the company.
The Silicon Valley company said these plans would support “Meta’s continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”.
Meta’s announcement came as other companies in the AI sector came under fire from Musk on Monday.
The tech entrepreneur said more than 200 neocloud firms were in trouble, which led to shares in Nebius, CoreWeave and Iren dropping in premarket trading on Monday. However, Iren and CoreWeave stock later recovered their losses, with Nebius closing more than 3% down.
“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,” the world’s richest person wrote in a post on X on Sunday.
Drawing an analogy with the survival prospects of the guppy fish – which has a reputation for struggling to thrive in domestic fish tanks – Musk added: “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many.”
The chief executive and largest shareholder of Tesla and SpaceX – which also owns and operates datacentres – was responding to a post by the venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya, who had written on the Musk-owned platform that neoclouds were “disorganized and poorly capitalized”.
Fears over the financial stability of neocloud businesses are focused on their high levels of borrowing – approximately $35bn at CoreWeave, for example – and whether the AI market will grow fast enough to service it.
Neil Wilson, an analyst at the investment platform Saxo UK, said Musk’s comments “underscore the fears that there is just way too much debt” in the AI sector.
“Meta’s not going to struggle to service debts and can lean on equity raises to minimise debt, too. This is kind of exactly the point Musk made about SpaceX having all its earnings and is investment grade, which the neoclouds don’t have,” he said.
SpaceX reported on Monday that it had entered a $40bn deal with Apollo Global Management to lease chips to power AI datacentres.
CoreWeave’s chief executive, Michael Intrator, reportedly sent an internal memo to employees this month saying that some investors had not understood the $30bn company. The firm’s stock has declined in value by more than a third over the past month.
“When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally,” he wrote, according to Bloomberg.

indian-startups-dd9023d3cb.headline: Unacademy Cofounders Plan ₹700 Cr AI, Deeptech Fund
indian-startups-dd9023d3cb.fulltext: Unacademy cofounders Gaurav Munjal and Roman Saini are raising a ₹700 Cr venture capital fund to back AI and deeptech startups, less than two months after upGrad completed the acquisition of the edtech startup. Named Longshot Capital, the Category II AIF has secured commitments of around ₹250-300 Cr and is targeting its first close in January 2027, ET reported, citing sources. Munjal and Saini declined to comment on the development. The Bengaluru-based fund plans to invest in 25-28 startups at the seed and pre-Series A stages, with initial cheques of $500,000 to $1.5 Mn and a targeted ownership stake of 8-12%. Saini will run Longshot Capital full-time, while Munjal will be involved part-time alongside his role heading Unacademy. Both founders will serve as general partners of the investment firm. The fund plans to deploy its capital over three years and will invest in India-based startups as well as companies founded by entrepreneurs of Indian origin. Its investment mandate will span AI-led businesses and deeptech segments such as manufacturing, space, defence and robotics, rather than consumer brands and retail businesses, the report said. The fund will have a lifespan of 10-11 years, allowing it to back businesses with longer gestation periods, particularly in AI and deeptech, according to the report. Its prospective investors include startup founders, family offices and overseas institutions. The fund formalises more than a decade of angel investing by Munjal and Saini. The two have collectively invested over ₹25 Cr through more than 200 angel cheques in companies including Pine Labs, Dhan, Seekho, Ultrahuman, Snabbit, Swish, STAGE, and Third Wave Coffee. In August, the duo also invested in Superleap, an AI-native customer relationship management platform. The proposed fund comes amid growing investor interest in frontier technologies, with Indian AI startups raising $438 Mn across 28 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 265% YoY. Meanwhile, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals during the same period, up 176% YoY. Unacademy Founders’ Second Act The move adds Munjal and Saini to a growing group of startup founders transitioning from personal angel investments to institutional fund management. Snapdeal cofounders Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal raised ₹333 Cr in external capital for Titan Capital in 2024. Freshworks founder Girish Mathrubootham cofounded the AI-focused Together Fund, while CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti joined Singularity Growth as a general partner after his exit. Myntra founder Mukesh Bansal operates venture studio Meraki Labs. The latest development comes over a month after upGrad acquired Unacademy in an all-stock transaction valuing it at ₹1,955 Cr, more than 90% below its peak valuation of $3.4 Bn in August 2021. Founded in 2015 by Munjal, Saini and Hemesh Singh, Unacademy started as a YouTube channel before evolving into an online learning platform focused on competitive exam preparation. It raised around $880 Mn from investors including SoftBank, Peak XV Partners, Elevation Capital, General Atlantic, Temasek, and Tiger Global. The startup became a unicorn in September 2020 and reached its peak valuation of $3.5 Bn in 2021, amid a pandemic-led boom in edtech investments. However, the reopening of educational institutions and a slowdown in demand for online learning forced Unacademy to rethink its business strategy. Unacademy undertook multiple rounds of layoffs, cut cash burn and scaled down several verticals as it sought to move towards profitability. It also expanded into offline coaching centres to tap demand for in-person test preparation. Unacademy subsequently explored acquisition opportunities with multiple players, including Allen Career Institute, K-12 Techno Services and upGrad. Its earlier merger discussions with upGrad fell through over valuation differences before the two companies revived negotiations and signed a term sheet in March. The acquisition was completed in September. Meanwhile, Munjal, on X yesterday, pushed back on criticism against the risk appetite of Indian deeptech investors, highlighting that startups like Astrobase, Airbound and Sarvam AI have been able to raise large rounds in short time periods. He also noted that consumer tech companies like Groww, Eternal and Meesho, all of whom went public in recent years, have provided “spectacular outcomes”.

indian-startups-8d259fd9ca.headline: BioStack Nets $9.5 Mn To Build Training Datasets For Medical AI
indian-startups-8d259fd9ca.fulltext: AI-powered healthtech platform BioStack has raised $9.5 Mn (₹90.4 Cr) in its seed funding round led by Peak XV Partners, Afore Capital, DCVC, Emerson Collective, SV Angel, Verdict Capital, Streamlined Ventures, and Y Combinator. The startup plans to utilise the fresh capital to continue expanding its presence in the US and other international markets, including India, Brazil, and Argentina. A chunk of the capital will also be used to scale its tech stack and ramp up hiring across engineering and research teams. Founded in 2025 by Sanat Mishra and Parth Patwa, BioStack claims to be building the data infrastructure for the next generation of medical AI. It combines fragmented clinical information across systems such as electronic health records, medical imaging, clinical notes and medications. The startup then uses this data to create proprietary datasets for research, biotechnology, and the development and training of medical AI models. “We’re building the infrastructure that connects all of the clinical information and makes it useful, both for clinicians making decisions today and for the researchers and AI developers building the future of medicine,” said BioStack cofounder and CEO Mishra. BioStack currently works with multiple hospitals across the US, Brazil and Argentina. In India, it is also connecting cancer patients with an investigational cancer vaccine program. The startup also claims that it offers use cases such as AI model evaluation, disease modeling, biomarker discovery, patient stratification and treatment-response analysis. Besides offering custom workflows to protect patient privacy, the startup claims to have so far processed 10 Cr de-identified patient records, more than “several hundred thousand” fragmented X-Rays, MRIs and CT scans, and “several million” telehealth audio transcripts. For context, de-identified patient records are medical datasets that have had all personal and direct identifiers removed so that the individual cannot reasonably be linked to the data. The fundraise comes as India becomes a training ground to collect datasets for powering AI models and physical AI products. Startups are tapping India’s huge population to collect recordings of workers performing physical tasks, processing the footage, and selling the resulting datasets to frontier AI labs and robotics companies. For instance, the likes of Awign, Objectways and Human Archive are building pipelines to supply first-person footage of human activity to AI developers. Just a day ago, instant home services startup Pronto’s founder Anjali Sardana launched Provision Labs, a US-based venture to collect data for physical AI systems. At the heart of all this is the Indian AI training dataset, which is projected to become a $1.3 Bn opportunity by 2033.

india-deep-tech-799476db76.headline: This startup’s self-driving excavators help dig up $600M in new funding
india-deep-tech-799476db76.fulltext:
Bedrock Robotics has raised $600 million in a funding round that values the autonomous vehicle technology startup at $4.1 billion, marking a speedy ascent for the two-year-old company.
The Series C round, co-led by CapitalG and Emergence Capital, comes two months after the startup reached a key milestone: moving its autonomous excavators beyond testing and pilot programs and putting them to work on active construction sites.
Bedrock Robotics has developed a self-driving kit that can be retrofitted onto construction and other worksite vehicles. Excavators outfitted with Bedrock’s autonomous-driving tech are now commercially operating at a Nevada-based water treatment facility, an earthwork site run by Champion Site Prep in Texas, and a 1.2 million-cubic-yard civil sitework project with Zachry Construction Corporation.
Bedrock has raised nearly $1 billion since it was founded in 2024 by a group of autonomous vehicle and robotics industry veterans. Co-founder and CEO Boris Sofman previously led Waymo’s now-shuttered self-driving trucks program. Sofman also co-founded and led Anki Robotics, the maker of the popular Cozmo consumer robot, which shut down in 2019.
Other co-founders include Waymo veterans Kevin Peterson, Bedrock’s chief technology officer, and Ajay Gummalla, who serves as Bedrock’s vice president of engineering and infrastructure. Tom Eliaz, who previously worked at Segment and Twilio, is also a co-founder and VP of engineering and hardware.
The fresh capital will help Bedrock accelerate its transition to commercial work. The company plans to deploy its technology at more construction sites, while expanding the teams and infrastructure needed to support customers in the field.
“We have proven that fully autonomous excavators can perform real work of value alongside the crews and workflows already in place on job sites. The next challenge is delivering that capability to more contractors as a dependable part of how projects get built,” Sofman said in a statement.
Bedrock is particularly focused on autonomous excavators, in part because of a growing shortage of skilled operators. It takes five years or more to master operating an excavator, according to Bedrock. Meanwhile, a growing number of construction workers are approaching retirement age. The Associated Builders and Contractors, a national construction industry trade association, estimates that more than 40% of construction workers will retire in the next five years.
Bedrock is betting that the industry will increasingly turn to autonomous driving tech to help close that labor gap.
The startup’s newest partner is Haydon, an Arizona-based general contractor that plans to use Bedrock-equipped machines across a range of projects, including advanced manufacturing facilities, water and wastewater plants, data centers, and healthcare facilities.
New investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek participated in the round, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, and Nvidia.
The startup also announced two executive hires as it scales commercial operations. Amy Jones Satrom, a veteran of Amazon, Nuro, and Uber, has joined Bedrock as its vice president of operations. Lando Juarez, formerly head of legal for Uber’s autonomous mobility and delivery business, was hired as general counsel.

deep-tech-3f860f2dcb.fulltext:
HCLTech, Japan’s Rapidus open two semiconductor engineering centres in India
HCLTech and Japan’s Rapidus Corporation have inaugurated two semiconductor engineering development centres in India as part of a partnership to support the Japanese company’s next-generation semiconductor technology requirements.
The centres, located in Bengaluru and Hubli, Karnataka, will provide engineering capabilities spanning mask design, design infrastructure, process design kit development, design technology co-optimisation and layout design, HCLTech said in a statement on Monday.
The partnership will also focus on building a pipeline of Indian engineering talent to meet Rapidus’ evolving workforce requirements in Japan. The companies did not disclose the financial details of the partnership or the number of engineers expected to be hired.
Rapidus is a Japanese company developing and manufacturing advanced logic semiconductors, with a focus on next-generation chip technologies.
Focus on semiconductor engineering and talent
“Building a strong engineering ecosystem is essential as Rapidus advances our mission to establish next-generation semiconductor manufacturing capabilities in Japan,” said Atsuyoshi Koike, representative director and chief executive officer of Rapidus Corporation.
“Through this collaboration with HCLTech, we expect to access India’s growing pool of semiconductor engineering talent and establish dedicated development capabilities that complement our operations in Japan,” Koike said.
He added that the companies would work together to develop the technical expertise and resources required to support Rapidus’ long-term objectives.
HCLTech CEO and managing director C Vijayakumar said the partnership reflects growing strategic collaboration between India and Japan in the semiconductor sector.
“Advanced semiconductors will define the technologies of the next decade,” Vijayakumar said. The partnership would bring together Rapidus’ next-generation semiconductor ambitions and HCLTech’s engineering expertise to accelerate chip adoption and shorten time-to-market, he added.
The collaboration is aimed at supporting semiconductor engineering requirements through dedicated development capabilities in India, while helping Rapidus build the talent base needed for its operations in Japan.
HCLTech’s engineering capabilities
HCLTech, which operates across more than 60 countries and employs over 230,000 people, provides technology services and products across areas including engineering, artificial intelligence, cloud and digital transformation.
The company reported consolidated revenue of $14.8 billion for the 12 months ended September 2026, according to the release.
Rapidus aims to develop and manufacture advanced logic semiconductors. Its stated areas of focus include shortening development cycles in chip design, wafer processing and 3D packaging.

global-economics-45a02624b5.headline: Tata Motors completes Iveco acquisition to turbocharge global play
global-economics-45a02624b5.fulltext:
Ayaan KartikPublished27 Oct 2026, 12:31 AM IST
NEW DELHI: Tata Motors Ltd has completed the acquisition of Italian truckmaker Iveco Group, marking a major step in the Indian commercial vehicle giant’s expansion into global markets and new product segments. The deal comes after a 15-month process that faced delays and resistance from some minority shareholders over the offer price.
An update on the Italian stock exchange late on Monday, showed that the transaction had been completed after the tender offer for Iveco shares closed with nearly 88% of the shares tendered, paving the way for the integration of the two commercial vehicle businesses. The acquisition, first announced in July 2025, has an enterprise value of about $4.5 billion.
The increase in tendering on Monday suggested that Tata Motors had won over most shareholders who had not voted at the extraordinary general meeting (EGM) on 16 October. About 12% of shareholders voted against resolutions related to the deal, while 35% did not vote. About 53% voted in favour.
Tata Sons' chairperson Natarajan Chandrasekaran, Jaguar Land Rover's chief executive P.B. Balaji, and Tata Motors' managing director Girish Wagh are among the top executives set to join Iveco’s board.
The deal—initially expected to close by June but delayed owing to regulatory approvals—brings together two commercial vehicle makers with a combined annual sales volume of more than 540,000 vehicles and revenue of over $25 billion. The combined business will have a much wider geographic footprint, with Europe accounting for about half of sales, India 35% and the Americas the remaining 15%, as per its earlier disclosures.
Tata Motors had earlier noted that the acquisition will help it gain access to geographies and segments where its commercial vehicle business has had a limited presence.
Iveco has a strong position in Europe and is the third largest commercial vehicle maker in Latin America, while Tata Motors has a more established presence in India and parts of Africa. The companies also have complementary distribution networks in markets such as West Asia, creating scope to expand each other’s reach.
The acquisition will also give Tata Motors access to products that it does not currently offer at scale. These include heavy-duty deep-mining trucks and tractor-trailers, areas where Iveco has established capabilities.
As per its plans for Iveco integration conveyed to analysts last year, cost savings will be another key focus.
Tata Motors has identified opportunities to lower product development costs by using common platforms and engineering capabilities, while sourcing more components from Eastern Europe and Asia.
Analysts tracking the company said the two businesses spend about 40% of their research and development budgets on similar projects, creating scope to eliminate duplication once the businesses are integrated.
The opportunity comes at a time when Iveco has struggled for growth. The company reported revenue of €15.3 billion in 2024, down 4% from a year earlier, with roughly three-fourths of its revenue coming from Europe, where its business contracted by about 7%.
Tata Motors management has argued that the acquisition could generate synergies greater than those achieved through its acquisition of Jaguar Land Rover in 2008. The company has also said the deal could help its commercial vehicle business become more meaningful globally.
After the announcement of the deal, Tata Motors had faced questions from investors over the strategic rationale of buying a large overseas business just as its commercial vehicle arm was being separated from the passenger vehicle business.
The company also had to contend with opposition from some Iveco shareholders during the tender process.
Activist investor Petrus Advisers argued that Tata Motors’ offer undervalued Iveco and sought a higher price. Tata eventually raised its offer to €14.40 a share from €14.10, describing the increase as a goodwill gesture to compensate shareholders for delays in completing the transaction.
Tata Motors’ management remained confident that it would secure the required acceptance level despite the resistance, saying it expected voluntary tendering to cross the 80% threshold needed for the transaction to proceed towards full control and delisting.
With the acquisition now complete, the focus shifts from securing shareholder nod to executing the integration and delivering the promised benefits.

global-economics-89d24445ea.headline: Noel Tata disputes Tata Sons board minutes, says Chandrasekaran's reappointment should be deleted from official records.
global-economics-89d24445ea.fulltext:
The standoff at Bombay House flared up yet again on Monday, with Noel Tata urging Tata Sons to remove all reference to the reappointment of N. Chandrasekaran from its board meeting minutes, and accusing it of making a regulatory filing based on what he called an invalid resolution.
In a nine-page letter to Suprakash Mukhopadhyay, Tata Sons group company secretary and copied to all directors, the Tata Trusts chairman wrote that Tata Sons' filing made to the Registrar of Companies “presents a contested and void resolution as a concluded act of the board, and conveys a false impression to the public, to the company’s stakeholders and to its regulators.” Noel also questioned whether Venu Srinivasan, the Trusts’ other nominee on the board, should have cast the deciding vote on Chandrasekaran's appointment, citing Mint’s report on business dealings between TVS Motor Corp. and a company run by Chandrasekaran’s family members.
This is Noel’s fifth letter to Tata Sons since the 17 September board meeting where the Tata Sons board ignored his objection and approved Chandrasekaran for a third five-year term starting February 2027. The decision put the board of the group’s holding company at odds with Tata Trusts, which owns 65.9% of Tata Sons. Noel first wrote two letters on 18 September, followed by a third on 30 September and then on 8 October, according to an executive privy to the developments. In his 8 November letter objecting to the contents of the meeting's minutes, Noel had written: “The minutes must record what transpired at the meeting."
Minutes, recording still withheld
In Monday's letter, Noel said he still has not received the final or signed minutes of the meeting, nor any reply to his 8 October letter asking for corrections to the draft. In his last letter, he had said the draft did not include two conditions all six directors had agreed to before announcing the results: that Tata Sons would get a legal opinion on the reappointment, and that shareholders would first approve Chandrasekaran’s directorship.
In its official filing on 15 October, Tata Sons left out the specific rules of Chandrasekaran's reappointment, Mint reported on 19 October.
“It is unacceptable that, despite being a director of the company, I have not been furnished with a certified true copy of the resolution and have instead been constrained to rely on a version circulating in the public domain,” Noel wrote in the latest letter.
He said Tata Sons had not answered his requests on 30 September and 8 October seeking the meeting's audio and video recordings. “The recording is the only neutral record of what transpired, and there can be no legitimate reason to withhold it from a director who was present at the meeting and who has placed his objections on record,” he wrote.
Emails sent to Tata Sons and Noel seeking comment went unanswered.
Agenda gave no notice
Noel noted that neither the original nor the revised agenda for the 17 September meeting mentioned a resolution to reappoint the executive chairman. The resolution was moved under item 7, described as a “Debriefing from Nomination and Remuneration Committee”.
At the centre of the dispute are two rules in Tata Sons’ Articles of Association. Article 118 requires a selection committee to pick a chairman. None was formed this time. Noel says the article also applies to reappointments, as it did for Chandrasekaran’s previous one. The draft minutes shared with Tata Sons board members on 4 October say it applies to appointing a “new chairman”, according to an executive.
Tata Sons maintains it acted correctly under Article 121, which requires a majority of the Trusts’ nominee directors to approve the chairman’s appointment. Noel voted against and Srinivasan in favour, producing a tie that Harish Manwani, chair of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee, broke with a casting vote.
Noel rejected that reading again. “A casting vote arises only on an equality of the votes of the board as a whole and cannot supply that affirmative vote,” he wrote, adding that he would treat any resolution passed otherwise “as not passed”.
Hanno One and TVS Motor
The sharpest part of the 26 October letter concerns Hanno One Warehousing Pvt. Ltd, whose directors include Chandrasekaran’s wife, Lalitha, and son, Pranav. On 22 September, Mint first reported on Chandrasekaran's family members having business links with TVS Motor Co. Ltd, raising governance questions after a deciding vote by the automaker’s chairman-emeritus, Venu Srinivasan, won Chandrasekaran a new term. On 30 September, Mint reported a second business link, noting that Hanno One was working on a ₹330-crore industrial park in Karnataka to serve TVS Motor.
“A director who is called upon to evaluate the performance of the executive chairman and to vote on his reappointment, while a company which he leads has a continuing commercial relationship with the immediate family of the executive chairman, stands in the very position which these provisions address,” Noel wrote, referring to the Tata Code of Conduct.
He argued that Srinivasan should have disclosed the dealings and recused himself. “The participation of a conflicted director goes to the validity of the decision itself,” the 26 October letter said.
Tata Sons’ spokesperson has previously said Hanno One’s formation was disclosed in April 2025 to companies Chandrasekaran leads, and that the TVS Motor deal did not need disclosure to Tata Sons. Tata said he did not remember any such disclosure reaching the board.
In his letter, Noel said the legal opinions from former Chief Justice of India U.U. Lalit and former Supreme Court judge B.N. Srikrishna came only after the vote result was announced; so, they cannot be called independent. He added that Justice Lalit’s opinion was sought by Harish Manwani, Anita George and Venu Srinivasan, all of whom voted for the reappointment. “The querists were, in substance, seeking an opinion on the validity of their own votes,” Noel wrote.
Demands and notice
Noel's Monday letter gave Tata Sons seven days to provide the meeting's recording, minutes, and the agenda audit trail on the Board Web App; and all disclosures of interest filed by Chandrasekaran and Srinivasan; and the briefs given to the legal experts. He has also asked that the company inform the registrar in writing that the resolution’s validity is disputed. “Failing the above, I will have no alternative but to draw adverse inferences,” he wrote. The Board Web App is a secure online portal where Tata Group directors access board agendas and meeting documents.

Morning opening: Serbia wakes up to new reality after Vučić
Jakub Krupa
Serbia wakes up to a new reality this morning after a grassroots opposition movement led by students ousted the country’s former authoritarian president Aleksandar Vučić, raising hopes for a new opening in relations with the EU and other partners.
The latest CeSID projection suggested the students will have 140 seats in the new parliament, well clear of the 126 required for majority, with 103 for Vucic’s bloc. No other party crossed the 3% threshold, with national minority parties taking the remaining seven seats.
We are likely to get more reactions to the vote today, with international observers set to present their preliminary report on the vote in the early afternoon.
I will also pick up the latest on the first round of the presidential vote in Bulgaria, which saw a record-low turnout of just 22%. The second round will be held this Sunday.
Elsewhere, I will be looking for updates from France and Italy after another rocky weekend of protests. French PM Sébastien Lecornu is going to meet with the student unions in the afternoon for what could be pivotal talks on the future of the demonstrations.
And E5 defence ministers – that’s France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and the UK – are meeting in Paris for discussions on Ukraine. Oh, and Slovakia’s foreign minister Juraj Blanár is in Moscow for energy talks with Russia.
It’s Monday, 26 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
International observers issued an overall positive assessment of the Serbian election, despite major underlying structural issues on state capture, polarisation, and misuse of state resources that require urgent addressing in the future (15:10, 15:15, 15:19, 15:37, 15:54)
The largest domestic group of observers also urged the incoming new government to “re-establish the integrity of elections” as one of its top priorities (13:31).
The focus now shifts to the government formation process as we wait for the official results to kick off the constitutional timeline (16:31).
Former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić is seen as a possible future prime minister, but the consultative and decentralised nature of the student movement makes it tricky to pinpoint who will get the top job (17:17).
Several EU leaders offered their congratulations for the student movement as they hoped for renewed engagement between the EU and Serbia (10:21, 12:15).
Russia said it hoped for cooperation with the new Serbian authorities, despite their preferred candidate Aleksandar Vučić losing the election (11:18).
Elsewhere,
In France, it is make or break time for the government on high school protests, which continued over the weekend, with the government now expected to set out new proposals to address the key demands in the late afternoon (13:02).
Bulgaria will head to the polls this Sunday in a runoff of the presidential race, with the list of candidates narrowed to two main favourites (12:59).
Sweden shows how complicated the government formation process can get as it remains stuck in finding a new parliamentary majority, 43 days on from the election (12:50).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
One thing to watch out for is how the Student List will pick its top figures, including the next prime minister and their presidential candidate.
One of the key features of the movementso far is that everythinghas been covered by very extensive and time-consuming consultations with student plenum meetings across the country, including the vetting of all candidates on the electoral list.
That may, of course, not always be possible in the future given the urgency some decisions will demand. The students will quickly need to figure out how to streamline these decision-making processes and make them work at the pace governing demands.
It may be easier to run a similarly complex process to choose their presidential candidate, as there is still some time to go until the vote in late December, but less so when it comes to the top jobs in the government, starting from the prime minister, and his key ministers.
“There is almost certainly going to be a complex process. It will not be decided by a small group of people sitting somewhere in a room. It’s only a matter of how complicated it will be,” Nikola Burazer, programme director at the Belgrade-based thinktank Centre for Contemporary Politics explained.
“It will have to be sped up because the process of choosing candidates for the list actually took a long time, months, to finish … [and finished] literally one day before they submitted the list. So, it has to be shorter.”
And the constitutional deadlines (16:31) will “force them to choose their candidates more quickly,” Aleksandar Ivković, a researcher at the Centre for Contemporary Politics added.
Former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić, who in 2012 resigned two years into the job in protest against alleged interference with his independence,is widely seen as the frontrunner for the job of the prime minister, but let’s see what other names can come up and who can emerged unscathed through the vetting process.
“After people are done celebrating and thinking about what happened yesterday, we will focus a bit more on what’s coming up, and how the government will look. 24 hours ago that all seemed like a fantasy to us,” Burazer said.
In terms of next steps in Serbia, here is what we know for now.
We are still waiting for the final election results: more than 97% polling station are now counted, but there are some localised issues that may even, in extreme cases, prompt a revote in some individual polling stations.
None of this will affect the overall result, but may cause a delay of a week or two from today.
Once the results are published, the National Assembly needs to meet for the first time within 30 days – that gets us to early to mid-December at the latest – starting the 90 days deadline for forming the new government.
This in itself will be fascinating as we have no idea who could emerge as the next prime minister given the leaderless nature of the Student List. Expect lots of speculation on this in the coming weeks, with former central bank governor Dejan Šoškić often mentioned as a possible candidate.
It’s worth saying that given the Student List will have a majority in the new parliament, they are very unlikely to need to run the clock down, and so the process can be well accelerated: manyexperts expect the new government to take over in December at the latest.
That timing is convenient for one more reason: following Vučić’s resignation as president to run for parliament, Serbia must hold a presidential election to choose a new head of state before the end of the year (well, by 27 December).
A close Vučić ally, Ana Brbabić, is currently the acting president as the last speaker of the parliament. Once we have a new speaker – presumably from the Student List – he or she will take over that interim role from here until the new leader gets elected.
That should make for an exciting end to the year in Serbia, with all change at the top going into 2027.
Serbian election marred by 'grave misuse of public resources' and 'intimidation of voters,' observers say
The preliminary report from international observers is also now out in writing, if you fancy reading it in full.
“Serbia’s 25 October early parliamentary elections saw active citizen engagement, with high voter turnout and vigorous competition between two main contenders, but unfolded in an atmosphere of profound polarisation, with equality of campaign opportunities seriously compromised, international observers said in a preliminary statement released today.
Entrenched advantages enjoyed by the ruling party, including the grave misuse of public resources, together with intimidation and pressure on voters, alongside disruptions of campaign activities, further marred the electoral environment, the statement says.”
International observers warn of issues with social media's impact on elections
Ireland’s Eoghan Murphy, who heads the ODIHR’s mission, goes into much more detail than other politicians on various technical issues in Serbia.
He talks in detail about the abuse of state resources for campaigning purposes, instances of intimidation and confrontation during the campaign, and serious issues spotted on social media and in traditional media.
This last point is particularly relevant as it feels it could just as well apply to most countries with elections coming up.
He warns that online campaigning “remains largely unregulated,” with “no dedicated oversight mechanism, safeguards … or accountability.”
“We don’t know how social media platforms prioritise and amplify such content, which harms transparency, and this reinforces the need for oversight and for safeguards.”
Sounds familiar?
He also makes it very clear that Serbia’s state media were way too involved in the election, with “pronounced imbalances in exposure and treatment of contestants, contrary to its legal obligations and public service mandate.”
“Overall, most monitored broadcasters failed to provide voters with the substantive and impartial information necessary to make an informed choice.”
“The arrangements for voting abroad raised concerns about the disproportionate inconvenience of voters in certain countries due to the absence of clear and objective criteria regarding polling stations, locations, and voting hours.”
Austrian MEP Andreas Schieder, head of the European parliament’s mission, also flags this problem, and says “this needs to change in the future.”
Italian MP Pierro Fassino, head of the parliamentary assembly of Council of Europe’s delegation and an Italian MP in his own right, is up next.
He says the election took place in a “calm and responsible manner … despite the polarised” atmosphere, with the electoral process passing the assessment at 96% of the polling stations observed.
The press conference continues along these lines, so I will flag if anyone disagrees with this view – or say anything particularly exciting about their experience of monitoring the vote.
International observers conclude with preliminary 'positive' assessment of Serbia vote, despite major structural issues
Special coordinator and Luxembourgish MP Gilles Baum is now speaking at the presentation of the international observers’ preliminary verdict on the election.
He says the election “unfolded in the atmosphere of profound polarisation, with the equality of campaign opportunity seriously compromised” through “entrenched advantages enjoyed by the ruling party.”
He also talks about the suspected “misuse of state resources together with intimidation and pressure on voters, candidates and civil society, as well as disruption of campaign activities.”
He warns that despite previous recommendations, “widespread distrust in the integrity of the voter registration persisted.”
But the mission’s on the day observation concludes with “positive” assessment of all stages of the election day process “in the vast majority of polling stations observer.”
“Nevertheless, reported incidents of physical violence raised serious concerns, and some procedural shortcomings were noted,” he says.
The main group of international observers – including OSCE’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and the European parliament - is about to deliver their preliminary verdict on the Serbian election, with a press conference in Belgrade.
