agritech-ad58637f19.headline: India’s 2026 Monsoon 13% Below Normal; Southern Reservoirs 43% Below Average
agritech-ad58637f19.fulltext:
TL;DR: India received 759.4 mm of rainfall during the June–September 2026 monsoon, 12.6% below its long-period average. East and Northeast India recorded their lowest seasonal rainfall since 1901, while the South Peninsula received 24% less rain than normal. Although extremely heavy rainfall events rebounded to 388, southern reservoirs held 24.76 BCM against a ten-year average of 43.33 BCM. Historical records show repeated drought declarations in districts such as Ananthapuramu in Andhra Pradesh, while post-monsoon soil moisture remains below average in several states. Together, these indicators reveal an uneven monsoon impact and highlight areas requiring closer monitoring.
Context
India’s monsoon tells two stories this year. The country received 12.6% less rainfall than normal between June and September 2026, but the shortfall was far from uniform. Eastern and northeastern India received 26% less rain than average, while the southern peninsula recorded a 24% deficit.
The season began on a difficult note, with June rainfall nearly 40% below normal. July brought a brief recovery, with rainfall slightly above average, but the deficit returned in August and September. The rebound, in other words, did not erase the shortfall.
What does this mean for the land and the people who depend on the rain? The IMD had warned of a below-normal monsoon in May, when El Niño conditions were expected to develop. But the national rainfall deficit is only the starting point. To understand where drought risks are emerging, it is necessary to look beyond how much rain fell to where it fell, how long the dry spells lasted, and how much moisture remained in the soil.
Who compiles this data?
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) publishes rainfall data and monsoon forecasts, while the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (NCFC) monitors agricultural conditions using rainfall, soil moisture and satellite indicators. The India Drought Monitor, developed by IIT Gandhinagar’s Water and Climate Lab, tracks drought conditions using meteorological and satellite data.
Where can I download clean & structured data related to this?
Clean, structured datasets related to Indian rainfall, drought conditions, agriculture and water resources are available on Dataful.
Key Insights
India’s 2026 monsoon ranks among the weakest in decades, with sharp regional deficits
India received 759.4 mm of rainfall during the June–September 2026 southwest monsoon, just 87% of its long-period average (LPA). According to the IMD, this was the country’s fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall since 2001 and 13th-lowest since 1901. The national shortfall, however, conceals sharper regional deficits.
East and Northeast India received 1,016.3 mm, or 74% of its regional LPA, making it the lowest seasonal rainfall for the region since 1901. The South Peninsula received 542 mm, or 76% of its LPA, ranking fourth-lowest since 1901 and second-lowest since 2001. Northwest India received 94.1% of its LPA, while Central India recorded 97%, within the normal range.
The shortfall also affected the monsoon core zone, which includes much of India’s rain-fed agricultural area. It received 779.9 mm, which is below the lower limit of the normal category (782.8 to 881.2). Across India’s 36 meteorological subdivisions, 17 (42% of the area) recorded deficient rainfall, 18 (53%) received normal rainfall, and one, in Odisha (5%), recorded excess rainfall. At the district level, 282 of 741 meteorological districts (38% of total area) recorded below-normal rainfall, while 34 (5% of total area) received significantly below-normal rainfall. Another 312 districts (42% of total area) recorded normal rainfall, 90 (12% of total area) received excess rainfall, and 16 (2% of total area) recorded substantially above-normal rainfall.
Extremely heavy rainfall events rebound in 2026, driven by a July spike
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) classifies rainfall of 115.6–204.4 mm in 24 hours as very heavy and rainfall exceeding 204.4 mm as extremely heavy. During the June–September 2026 monsoon, India recorded 1,765 very heavy rainfall events and 388 extremely heavy events. Extremely heavy events rose from 296 in 2022 to 426 in 2023 and peaked at 473 in 2024, before declining to 303 in 2025 and increasing again in 2026. Very heavy rainfall events followed a different trend, rising from 1,875 in 2022 to a peak of 2,632 in 2024, before falling to 2,109 in 2025 and 1,765 in 2026. July 2026 alone recorded 269 extremely heavy events, the highest July count in since 2022, compared with 84 in 2025. These figures show that although the overall frequency of very heavy rainfall has declined since 2024, extremely heavy events rebounded in 2026.
Historical El Niño years show a recurring concern, but widely varying rainfall outcomes
Historical data in the IMD’s El Niño table show why the phenomenon matters when assessing India’s 2026 monsoon, but also why it cannot explain the season’s outcome on its own. Of the 17 El Niño years listed between 1951 and 2023, 12 recorded below-normal June–September rainfall, including seven with deficits exceeding 10%. Yet outcomes varied considerably: rainfall was 22.3% below normal in 1972 and 20.9% below normal in 2002, while 1994 recorded a 13.9% surplus and 1997 ended almost exactly at normal, despite being the only Strong El Niño among all.
Monthly figures reveal another important distinction. In 2002, July rainfall was 50.6% below normal, contributing to a seasonal deficit of 20.9%. In 2023, above-normal rainfall in July and September partly offset August’s 36.1% shortfall, leaving the season 5.3% below normal. A seasonal total can therefore conceal sharp monthly swings, just as a national average can mask regional rainfall deficits.
That distinction is relevant to the 2026 monsoon. India received 759.4 mm of rainfall, or 87% of its long-period average, with particularly large deficits in East and Northeast India and the South Peninsula. IMD reported that El Niño strengthened during the season, but the historical comparisons do not establish how much it contributed to this year’s shortfall. Nor does deficient seasonal rainfall alone establish the severity of agricultural drought.
Southern reservoirs fall to less than half their year-ago levels
The clearest concentration of pressure appears in the reservoir data. On 15 October, CWC’s 178 monitored reservoirs nationally held 68.58% of their live-storage capacity. Their storage was 16.44% below the corresponding ten-year average. Of the 178 reservoirs monitored by the Central Water Commission, on 15 October 2026, 105 held more than 80% of their ten-year average storage, while 73 were at or below that level. Of the latter, 31 had storage at or below 50% of normal.
The shortfall was concentrated in the South. Its 50 monitored reservoirs held 24.76 BCM, against a ten-year normal of 43.33 BCM, a deficit of 18.57 BCM. This accounts for approximately 74.5% of the net national storage shortfall of 24.93 BCM, including the effect of a small surplus in Central India.
State-level departures varied considerably. Storage was 61.50% below normal in Tamil Nadu, 59.33% in Andhra Pradesh and 51.63% in Telangana. Karnataka was 32.28% below normal, while Kerala was 17.67% below. These figures indicate a weaker reservoir position, but do not translate directly into equivalent reductions in water available to every user. Actual supply depends on the reservoirs serving an area, existing commitments, alternative sources and distribution systems.
The timing is also important. Tamil Nadu receives a substantial share of its rainfall during the October–December northeast monsoon, making subsequent rainfall and reservoir inflows important to watch. The 15 October 2026 figures are therefore a snapshot, not a final assessment of water availability for the coming months. Even so, the regional imbalance is clear: the national storage figure masks the depth of the shortfall in southern India.
District data show where rainfall deficiency meets underlying drought vulnerability
It is also important to look at districts apart from broad regions. IMD’s seasonal rainfall distribution records 282 districts with deficient rainfall and 34 with large-deficient rainfall. Together, that is 316 districts, or approximately 42.6% of the 741 districts listed. Further, 312 districts are recorded in the normal category, 90 with excess rainfall and 16 with large-excess rainfall. The distribution confirms that the deficient season was far from uniform. It also needs to be interpreted precisely: a rainfall-deficient district is not automatically a district officially declared drought-hit.
The agriculture ministry’s Crisis Management Plan (CMP) for drought provides a list of districts where state governments declared drought from 2011-12 to 2025-26. It has 472 districts declared drought over the years, and such declarations peaked in 2015-16 with 294 districts declared drought-affected, and in recent years, it declined: 71 in 2023-24 (Karnataka 31, Maharashtra 15, Rajasthan 12, Andhra Pradesh 13), and only 5 in 2024-25 and 4 in 2025-26, all in Andhra Pradesh. Ananthapuramu was declared drought-affected in 11 years, followed by Barmer, Jaisalmer, Bellari and 14 other districts with declarations in 10 years each.
A separate 2024 district risk assessment by the Department of Science and Technology identifies underlying vulnerability. It places 91 districts in the very high drought-risk category and 188 in the high category, 279 districts in total. More than 90% of districts in the Very High category (83 out of 91) are located in Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, and Maharashtra. These classifications combine hazard, exposure and vulnerability. They identify relative structural risk, rather than establishing that all these districts experience drought. The left image provides the Drought exposure Map, while the right image shows the current drought conditions as on 21st October, 2026, according to the India Drought Monitor.
Root-Zone Soil Moisture overlaps with low reservoir storage levels in Southern India
The NCFC’s report dated 19 October 2026 provides a more recent indicator of agricultural conditions. It compares root-zone soil moisture for 8–14 October with the average for the previous ten years.
The report finds that root-zone soil moisture was similar to or better than the ten-year average in parts of Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh, eastern and northern Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. In contrast, soil moisture was below the ten-year average in Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and the Northeast region.
The comparison suggests that the effects of the monsoon deficit were not uniform across the country and that some areas entered the post-monsoon period with less soil moisture than their historical average. For agriculture, root-zone moisture is particularly relevant because it reflects water availability in the soil where plant roots draw moisture.
The overlap between below-average soil moisture and low reservoir storage in parts of southern India warrants particular attention. At the same time, soil moisture at or above the historical average in parts of eastern and central India shows why a national rainfall deficit cannot be used as a proxy for conditions in every district.
The coming weeks will bring further evidence about how these conditions develop. In Tamil Nadu, the northeast monsoon and associated reservoir inflows will be especially relevant. Elsewhere, changes in soil moisture and water storage will help clarify whether the seasonal rainfall deficit translates into continuing agricultural or water-supply pressure.

The scale of the opportunity is already significant. India has 2,117 active GCCs, employing 2.36 million professionals and contributing $98.4 billion in annual revenue.
Also Read: India's manufacturing and services sectors are projected to generate more than 35 crore new jobs by 2030: Report
What stands out now is a shift in activity in these centres. As much as 44% of GCCs have reached the portfolio hub or transformation stage where they increasingly own platforms, products, AI adoption and business-critical outcomes. AI is the engine behind this shift. India has more than 250,000 AI/ML talent and more than 1,200 AI-enabled GCCs, marking its lead in global AI hiring. Also, 83% of GCCs are scaling GenAI, 70% are following a hybrid AI model and 58% are investing in agentic AI, which shows GCCs are no longer just executing for global enterprises but helping drive their transformation.
“The GCC story in India is no longer about where work gets done,” said Neeti Sharma, CEO, TeamLease Digital. “It is about who shapes what global enterprises build next. As these centres take on the thinking, ownership and accountability behind AI, India is becoming central to how enterprises across the world transform.”
Also Read: Poor management, toxic workplace culture outweigh salary in job-change decisions: Report
“The next phase of GCC growth will be led less by scale of headcount and more by judgment, governance and the ability to turn AI into business outcomes,” said Sharma. “The task for India now is to build talent at that depth, so that GCCs remain not just an execution hub for global enterprises, but a source of their innovation and strategic capability.”
As GCCs take on more ownership, the enabling talent is also getting rewarded. The 2026 salary increment in GCCs is at 10.4%, ahead of the 9.1% India Inc average. AI, ML, cyber and cloud skills carry a 30–40% pay premium because demand outpaces supply.
The AI talent landscape identified by TeamLease Digital showed this premium is spread unevenly across roles. Depth is concentrated in AI-core, roles that build and own intelligent systems, which appears in only two places: the AI family and AI risk governance. Breadth sits in AI-adjacent roles, which apply AI within established workflows and span data, cloud and cybersecurity. No AI-support role appears at premium in a GCC, indicating that the routine layer is being repriced downward rather than upward.
The salary findings showed that this divide begins at entry itself. For early and mid-career roles, at 0–2 years of experience, AI-core roles earn a median fixed pay of ₹10.8 lakh per annum (LPA) for a data scientist) to ₹13.2 LPA for GenAI engineer). AI-adjacent roles earn ₹9.0 LPA (cybersecurity engineer) to ₹10.2 LPA (data engineer), while AI-support roles earn ₹4.8 LPA (data quality analyst) to ₹5.4 LPA (application support engineer). AI-core roles therefore open 2.5–3× above AI-support, and they are also projected to grow faster, at 16–21% against 7–8%.
The findings also pointed to where salary growth is headed in FY28. GenAI, ML and data science remain the highest-return skilling pathways for salary acceleration in GCCs. Skills in LLMs, RAG, and prompt engineering, are projected to grow 20.5% in FY27–28, followed by ML skills such as PyTorch, TensorFlow and model deployment at 18.7%. At senior levels, LLM architecture, RAG at scale, and agentic AI lead at 20.8%, followed by AI architecture, MLOps, GenAI strategy and model governance at 19.6%.

other-interests-c328a45aaf.headline: Satellites show some of the strongest evidence the AMOC is weakening
other-interests-c328a45aaf.fulltext:
Satellite measurements suggest the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) has been transporting less heat towards Europe, providing some of the strongest evidence yet of a slowdown in these ocean currents, which keep Europe’s climate mild.
The AMOC system of currents, which includes the Gulf Stream, brings warm, salty water from the Gulf of Mexico to the north Atlantic, where it cools and sinks, returning south along the sea floor.
As it cools, the water releases heat into the atmosphere. But based on the satellite data, Richard Allan at the University of Reading, UK, and his colleagues calculated that the heat flux out of the north Atlantic has decreased 18 per cent in 40 years.
Advertisement
Because the AMOC’s flow varies from year to year, the scientists used the first decade of data to estimate an average flow. They compared this to the following decades to find the circulation has declined 14 per cent in 30 years.
“We expect the AMOC to deliver heat northwards, and then that heat to come out of the top of the ocean into the atmosphere, and so if one of those things is changing, we expect the other one to change,” says Neil Fraser at the Scottish Association for Marine Science, who wasn’t involved in the study. “This is some of the strongest evidence so far that the AMOC has weakened over the last 40 years.”
Climate models suggest the surge of fresh water from the melting Greenland ice sheet will dilute the salty water of the AMOC and slow its sinking, weakening the circulation. Some research suggests the AMOC could collapse as soon as 2060, plunging Europe into “ice age” winters with stronger storms and widespread drought.
Ocean buoys across the Atlantic have measured changes in water pressure corresponding to about a 10 per cent decline in AMOC strength since 2004, but because its flow can sometimes ebb for decades at a time, this doesn’t prove a long-term trend.
Scientists have looked for indirect evidence, like the “cold blob” in the north Atlantic, the only area of the world that has cooled since the 1800s. A 2018 analysis of these declining sea-surface temperatures estimated the AMOC had weakened 15 per cent since the 1950s.
But sea-surface temperatures could also be decreasing due to a shift in jet stream winds or increased shading by clouds. Heat flux from the north Atlantic to the atmosphere can be a better indicator as it is “one step closer to the thing that drives AMOC”, says David Thornalley at University College London.
Last year, a study calculated this heat flux from atmospheric reanalyses, which are essentially computer models that are nudged to match the spotty real-world observations on record. But the results didn’t show any decline in AMOC strength between 1963 and 2017.
The new study, which is undergoing peer review, is the first to estimate AMOC weakening with heat fluxes calculated in part from satellite measurements, according to Allan. For decades, the ratio between how much solar energy Earth receives and how much heat energy it radiates back into space has been growing more positive. The researchers combined satellite measurements of this energy imbalance with reanalyses and models to figure out how much less heat the north Atlantic has been releasing to the atmosphere.
“The resulting inferred net air-sea flux is of demonstrably better quality than other estimates, making this estimate more suitable to infer AMOC changes,” says team member Michael Mayer at the University of Vienna.
And because satellite measurements can be updated regularly, this method, if it holds up to scrutiny, could someday “provide a new early warning method for detecting changes in this vital current”, says Allan. The UK is investing £81 million in research to build an early warning system for AMOC collapse by 2030, although this study isn’t part of the initiative.
Stefan Rahmstorf at the University of Potsdam, Germany, argues that heat flux isn’t necessarily a better indicator of AMOC changes than sea-surface temperatures, which can be directly measured. But he says the two build on each other to increase concern that the AMOC could be approaching a tipping point.
Another recent study, which examined reanalyses of the ocean rather than the atmosphere, similarly found the AMOC has weakened 15 per cent in 30 years.
“The strongest evidence is the combination of several different lines of evidence, all pointing to a slowing AMOC,” says Rahmstorf.

world-78a8c8b9b9.headline: Face-Offs at India-China Border Are Continuing at Multiple Points, ITBP Chief Confirms
world-78a8c8b9b9.fulltext:
Claims by civil society groups and media in India’s northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh that Chinese troops have been crossing into Indian territory, which the Narendra Modi government has repeatedly denied, were confirmed by a top Indian official last week.
At an event in Alwar, Rajasthan, on October 22, Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur said that face-offs are happening between Indian and Chinese forces “at several locations in Arunachal and it still continues.”
Kapur’s remarks on Thursday about the face-offs are hardly a revelation. Civil society groups and media in the northeast Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, which borders China, have been drawing attention to the fragile, even alarming situation along the frontier since June-July.
In a letter dated June 26, 2026, to the deputy commissioner of Upper Subansiri, the Nah Welfare Society (NWS) said that the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) had occupied Indian territory in and around Taksing, including Oying in the Asaphila area, Paniar in the Chujarta area, Marpan in Marnafe, Portrang Lake, and Tingdingtang. In addition to establishing a military camp in the area, the PLA has also built roads, bridges, and military camps in several locations traditionally used by local communities for grazing, hunting, and collecting forest produce. A Taksing-based tribal organization, the NWS expressed “deep grief” over the PLA’s gradual occupation of ancestral lands, which it said, has intensified since 2020.
Soon after the contents of the NWS’ memorandum became public, the Indian Army categorically dismissed the “reports” as “incorrect and without any basis.” Then came videos claiming the PLA had advanced 50-60 km into Indian territory. The Indian government’s Press Information Bureau Fact Check unit dismissed the reports as ” fake;” the videos did not pertain to the India-China border, it said. This was followed by reports and videos of “skirmishes” in the Taksing Circle on July 25-26. The “confrontation” reportedly “continued for nearly a week before the situation was brought under control following intervention by senior commanders from both sides.” However, Arunachal Pradesh’s Home Minister Mama Natung dismissed the reports of Chinese encroachment as “just rumors.”
Now, for the first time, there is official confirmation of confrontations at multiple locations along the India-China border in Arunachal Pradesh. And this confirmation has come from the head of the ITBP, the force that guards the India-China border.
The entire India-China border is disputed. The two countries not only have differing perceptions of where the Line of Actual Control, the de facto border, runs, but they also claim swathes of territory under the other’s control. China claims 90,000 sq km of territory that roughly coincides with Arunachal Pradesh. India claims 38,000 sq km of territory in Aksai Chin that China occupied during the 1962 border war, and another 5,300 sq km in the Shaksgam Valley of Jammu and Kashmir that Pakistan occupied in 1947-48 and gifted to China in 1963.
Besides the war in 1962, which China won, the two sides have engaged in skirmishes and standoffs several times over the decades, including at Samdurong Chu in Arunachal in 1986-87, at the Doklam trijunction of China, India and Bhutan in 2017, and at Galwan in Ladakh in June 2020, which resulted in the death of 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese soldiers.
Interestingly, China’s interest in Arunachal Pradesh has waxed and waned over time. After occupying Arunachal, then known as the North East Frontier Agency, for several weeks during the 1962 war, the PLA pulled out. Indeed, it did not seem interested in pressing any claims here, and under a swap proposal, was willing to give up claims in the eastern sector, in return for India accepting its control over Aksai Chin in the western sector.
It was only from the mid-1980s that China began reasserting claims over what it calls “Zangnan” or “South Tibet,” at bilateral talks, through military intrusions, by pushing back Indian patrol teams, objecting to visits of Indian leaders to Arunachal Pradesh, refusing to issue visas to Indian passport holders from the state on the argument that they are not Indian, and announcing “standardized” or Chinese names for places and geographical features in the state. According to a 2025 Pentagon report, Arunachal Pradesh is among China’s “core interests.”
In recent months, India and China have engaged in a slew of talks. On August 6, the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on India-China Border Affairs was held in New Delhi. Then on August 26, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval met with China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi at the 25th round of Special Representatives’ talks on the Boundary Question in Beijing. On September 6, the Indian Army and the PLA held their first Corps Commander-level meeting in the Eastern Sector at the Vacha-Damai Border Personnel Meeting Point in Arunachal Pradesh.
India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping shook hands and chatted at the SCO Summit at Bishkek on August 31, and held a meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in Delhi on September 12.
If the India-China face-offs are continuing, as the ITBP Director General Kapur said they are, it is clear the talks have had little impact in deterring the PLA.
One obvious reason is that Prime Minister Modi’s China strategy is guided more by his interest in beefing up his image among his supporters than taking a strong position against China. His government has repeatedly denied PLA encroachment into Indian controlled territory. “Neither is anyone inside our territory nor is any of our post captured,” Modi grandly declared at an all-party meeting days after the Galwan clashes. The recent spate of denials by the government over PLA’s encroachments in Arunachal is part of the same short-sighted vision. It has weakened India’s hand at talks.
Even more baffling is the Modi government’s withdrawal of ITBP companies from the border. Since June-July, massive anti-government protests in the capital have rattled the Modi government. In response, it has pulled out ITBP personnel from the India-China border and redeployed them in Delhi at a time when the border situation is volatile. Clearly, using the ITBP to crush unarmed civilian protestors in Delhi is more important to Modi than using the force to push back PLA advances at the Arunachal border.
Under the BJP government, almost every Indian state/union territory bordering China is roiled in unrest. Arunachal’s civil society has strongly opposed a mega dam being constructed in the state’s Upper Siang district. The state’s inept handling of public concerns raised over displacement, environmental impact, and loss of livelihoods, and its use of force to deal with protests have resulted in the escalation of the conflict. On October 23, Upper Siang witnessed unprecedented scenes of violence.
Already, Arunachalis are upset with the government for not acting on their apprehensions over PLA encroachment into their traditional lands and hunting grounds. Delhi’s use of the iron fist now to put down their protests will fuel further anger. This will only add to India’s troubles in a sensitive border region.

global-economics-4d50d8833b.headline: Microsoft to offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in India, US, UK and Canada as it restructures workforce for AI
global-economics-4d50d8833b.fulltext:
LivemintPublished26 Oct 2026, 11:45 PM IST
Microsoft Corp. will offer buyouts to around 60,000 employees as the technology giant seeks to reduce costs and restructure its workforce to adapt to the artificial intelligence (AI) era.
The offer will be available to certain employees in the US, Canada, India and the UK at the vice president level and below, a Microsoft spokesperson said.
According to people familiar with the terms, divisions such as Xbox, Windows, Copilot and finance will fully participate in the buyout programme.
However, certain groups of employees will be excluded from the offer. These include some workers involved in data centres, sales, marketing, cybersecurity and quantum computing, the people said. Microsoft declined to comment on these specific details.
In a note to employees on Monday, Chief People Officer Amy Coleman said the programme would give eligible workers an opportunity to leave the company with support.
“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,” Coleman said.
A Microsoft spokesperson said employees who accept the offer would receive benefits similar to those provided under a standard severance package.
The latest buyout programme comes as Microsoft has reduced its workforce through multiple rounds of job cuts in recent years.
In July, the company offered buyouts to employees approaching retirement age. More than 30% of the approximately 8,750 employees eligible for that programme accepted the offer.
However, Microsoft expects significantly fewer employees to accept the latest buyout proposal than the voluntary retirement programme, the spokesperson said.
Microsoft’s headcount as of the end of June was 223,000. The figure has been largely flat since 2022, about the time Microsoft began spending heavily on AI and data centers — squeezing budgets and hiring elsewhere in the company.
The company is scheduled to report financial results on Wednesday, and investors will be laser-focused on signs that the heavy spending on AI is paying off. Microsoft shares rose about 1% at midday in New York.
Other companies have sought to shrink headcount as they redirect spending to AI infrastructure. Google offered voluntary buyouts in a number of units last year, CNBC reported. Meta Platforms Inc.’s headcount is down by more than 20,000 from a late 2022 peak. Both are among the biggest spenders on data center infrastructure.
The Microsoft spokesperson said the company wants employees who are engaged on the hard problems it’s trying to solve. That echoes other tech bosses, who’ve publicly made clear that continued employment means embracing a faster pace of work and change.
Elon Musk in 2022 famously gave Twitter employees the choice to be “extremely hardcore,” or take a severance payment. Earlier this year, Business Insider reported that a Google executive told employees in his organization that those who weren’t “all in” on AI could have a voluntary buyout package.
Workers deciding whether to take a buyout typically assess their savings and whether they’re at risk of layoffs later. Midcareer professionals also consider the job market and how long it might take them to find a new role, or whether the package gives them enough runway to make a pivot. Buyouts typically go to more senior, higher-cost staff, as with Microsoft’s round of early retirement offers, and offer more generous terms than a layoff.
In some cases, Microsoft will try to retain top talent if employees opt to take the buyout offer, the spokesperson said.
The buyouts give Microsoft units “another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs,” Coleman wrote in the memo.

work-careers-294311995a.headline: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees in India, US, UK and Canada; HR head Amy Coleman tells staff
work-careers-294311995a.fulltext:
Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees across India, the US, the UK and Canada, its second voluntary exit programme this year and a much wider one than the first. Announced on Monday in a memo from Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, the Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) covers more than a quarter of the company's roughly 223,000 employees. It reaches up to level 70 on Microsoft's internal scale, which takes in general managers and some staff with vice president titles, though not corporate vice presidents.
Unlike the retirement buyout Microsoft ran earlier this year, this one has no age or tenure cut-off, and performance plays no part in who qualifies. Eligible employees will get an email with their individual terms within hours. They have until the first week of December to decide, and those who accept will leave at the end of the year.
"This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support,"
 Coleman wrote. It also gives participating organisations 
"another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs,"
 she added.
Microsoft's voluntary exit offer pays out like its standard severance
The package matches Microsoft's standard severance. That means base pay linked to tenure and level, continued stock vesting, healthcare for a fixed period and career transition support. What it leaves out is the extended healthcare that made the retirement programme an easy yes for many long-serving staff.
Severance in Microsoft's US layoffs earlier this year started at 60 days of base pay and went up to 39 weeks for most employees. Staff at level 64 and below got a week of base pay for every six months of service, while levels 65 to 67 got two weeks.
Not every team is in. Business leaders decide whether their groups participate, and sales is sitting this one out. Marketing, commercial business, security, and discovery and quantum teams are excluded too, according to people familiar with the matter. Copilot, CoreAI, Windows + Devices, Xbox, finance and HR are among those taking part, while Cloud + AI and Microsoft AI are partially in.
Buyouts now sit alongside layoffs in Microsoft's AI-era job cuts
The VEO builds on the Voluntary Retirement Program from this spring, the first in Microsoft's history. That offer went to roughly 8,750 US employees at senior director level and below whose age and years at the company added up to at least 70. About 30% took it, and Microsoft booked a $900 million charge for it in April.
The turnout helped shrink the layoffs that followed, Coleman said later. Microsoft still cut 4,800 jobs in July, about 2% of its workforce, and several hundred more in September, after cutting over 15,000 in 2025. Headcount stood at 223,000 on June 30, down from 228,000 a year earlier.
The company is under pressure to hold down operating costs while it spends tens of billions on data centres and AI infrastructure. Still, Microsoft says the buyout is not a sign it needs fewer people, nor a replacement for layoffs, which remain on the table. It expects a much smaller share of employees to accept this time.
Quarterly earnings on Wednesday could offer a first look at what the offer will cost. Coleman called the programme "new for us" in her memo, and said in July that Microsoft was studying whether voluntary exits could become a regular, even annual, fixture. How many of these 60,000 employees take the deal will likely settle that.

india-deep-tech-3bd53519fa.headline: Intel to acquire Israeli quantum startup Classiq for $2.3 billion in record deal
india-deep-tech-3bd53519fa.fulltext:
Intel is acquiring Israeli quantum computing startup Classiq for $2.3 billion in a combination of cash and shares, Calcalist reported Monday, in what would be the largest acquisition of a quantum computing company to date. The deal represents a major milestone for Israel's emerging quantum technology industry, where companies have attracted substantial investment despite the technology's limited commercial adoption. 
Founded in 2020, Classiq develops software designed to make quantum computers easier to program and operate. Rather than building quantum hardware itself, the company focuses on the software connecting complex quantum systems with the businesses and researchers seeking to use them. Its ambition is to provide the equivalent of a Windows operating system for quantum computing.
The company was founded by CEO Nir Minerbi, Chief Product Officer Amir Naveh and his father, Chief Technology Officer Yehuda Naveh. Minerbi and the younger Naveh are graduates of the Israeli military's elite Talpiot technological training program, while Yehuda Naveh previously held a senior position at IBM's Israeli research and development operations.
Classiq currently employs approximately 150 people and has raised around $200 million since its establishment. Its most recent major funding round, in 2025, valued the company at approximately $600 million to $700 million, making Intel's purchase price more than three times that valuation.
The acquisition is also expected to generate substantial payouts for employees. According to Calcalist, employees collectively own approximately 10% of Classiq, representing around $230 million at the transaction valuation. Intel has reportedly allocated more than $100 million in additional retention grants. The company's three founders are each expected to receive between $80 million and $100 million. 
Among the major investors are Entrée Capital, Team8 Capital and Israeli insurer Phoenix. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan is also a personal investor in Classiq, having acquired his stake before becoming Intel's chief executive. According to sources close to the Israeli company, Tan did not participate in the acquisition negotiations because of his financial interest.
The acquisition comes as quantum computing companies compete to develop commercially viable applications for technology that remains expensive and difficult to scale. Classiq already works with customers including BMW, Rolls-Royce, HSBC and Citi, although its annual revenue remains below $100 million.
Until recently, Classiq had been considering a Wall Street listing through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC. Instead, the Intel deal offers its shareholders an exit at a valuation that places it among the world's most valuable quantum computing businesses. 
For Intel, the transaction marks its largest significant acquisition in Israel since its approximately $1 billion purchase of transportation technology company Moovit in 2020. For Israel's quantum sector, it provides a major financial benchmark in an industry where expectations of future breakthroughs have so far run well ahead of widespread commercial adoption.

india-deep-tech-a9e4c1df42.headline: Intel to acquire Israeli quantum startup Classiq for $2.3 billion
india-deep-tech-a9e4c1df42.fulltext:
Intel to acquire Israeli quantum startup Classiq for $2.3 billion
The deal marks a record acquisition in the quantum computing industry and a major exit for Israel’s tech sector, with Classiq’s founders, employees and early investors poised for substantial returns.
The first major exit for Israel’s quantum industry: Classiq, a developer of operating systems for quantum computers, is being acquired by Intel for $2.3 billion in a combination of cash and stock. The deal would make Classiq the most expensive quantum company acquisition to date, by a significant margin. The previous record was set last year, when IonQ acquired Oxford Ionics for $1 billion.
The transaction also marks a major acquisition for Intel, which paid approximately $1 billion for Israeli mobility company Moovit six years ago and $2 billion for Habana Labs a year earlier. Intel has made other acquisitions since then, including the Israeli company Granulate, but those deals were valued in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Intel has not acquired another Israeli company since the Granulate deal in 2022.
For Israelis accustomed to multibillion-dollar exits in cybersecurity, $2.3 billion might not seem particularly large. In quantum computing, however, it represents a landmark deal. Despite the excitement surrounding the field, quantum computers have yet to achieve widespread practical commercial use. There are currently only 117 quantum computers worldwide, and they remain prohibitively expensive and largely inaccessible.
Quantum computing has shown promise for decades, and the field has recorded several significant breakthroughs over the past two years. Yet it has not experienced its own “ChatGPT moment,” a breakthrough that would bring the technology into widespread use.
Despite its small size, Israel is considered one of the world’s five leading countries in quantum computing, both in the number of companies operating in the field and in the volume of private investment. Intel’s acquisition of Classiq for more than $2 billion could draw greater investor attention to Israel and provide another catalyst for the development of its quantum industry.
The deal recalls Intel’s acquisition of Mobileye, the autonomous-driving company founded by Amnon Shashua, a decade ago. That transaction helped trigger a wave of investment in Israeli companies in the sector. The hope is that Classiq’s exit will have a similar effect, with even better long-term results for the industry.
For Classiq’s founders, employees and investors, the acquisition represents an impressive exit for a company founded just six years ago. Classiq currently employs around 150 people. Employees collectively hold 10% of the company’s shares, equivalent to $230 million at the acquisition price, although the proceeds will vary among individuals. Intel has also allocated more than $100 million in retention grants to encourage employees to remain with the company.
Classiq was founded by Nir Minerbi, Amir Naveh and his father, Prof. Yehuda Naveh. Minerbi is the CEO, Amir Naveh is the CPO, and Yehuda Naveh is the CTO. Minerbi and the younger Naveh are graduates of the Israel Defense Forces’ Talpiot program, as are many of the company’s employees. Yehuda Naveh previously held a senior position at IBM’s Israeli development center. Each of the three founders is expected to receive between $80 million and $100 million from the deal.
Classiq generates revenue, but its annual revenue remains in the tens of millions of dollars, well below an annual run rate of $100 million. The acquisition price therefore represents a substantial valuation multiple for a relatively young company.
Classiq occupies a distinctive position in the quantum computing industry. It develops software that serves as an operating system for quantum computers, bridging the gap between complex hardware and the people and organizations seeking to use it. The company’s ambition is to become the “Windows” of quantum computing.
IBM, a pioneer in quantum computing, is its main competitor. Estimates suggest that Classiq has already surpassed IBM in market share, although the companies’ positions depend on how that market is measured. Classiq’s software is hardware-agnostic, meaning it is designed to work across different quantum computing platforms rather than being tied to a single manufacturer.
Its customers span several industries, including banking, automotive and pharmaceuticals. They include BMW, Rolls-Royce, HSBC, Deloitte, Toshiba and Citi.
Classiq has raised approximately $200 million to date, making the acquisition a profitable outcome for its investors as well. Its most recent funding round, a $110 million raise in 2025, valued the company at an estimated $600 million to $700 million, far below the acquisition price.
Entrée Capital, which led Classiq’s pre-seed round and is its largest shareholder, stands to gain the most. The fund is expected to receive more than $300 million on an investment of just a few million dollars. Team8 Capital, the company’s second-largest shareholder, holds a 9% stake.
The deal is also expected to benefit Israeli savers through The Phoenix, which holds a 7.5% stake in Classiq. Unlike many recent Israeli technology exits, most of which have involved cybersecurity companies, Classiq is incorporated in Israel. The state is therefore expected to collect tax revenue from the transaction beyond the taxes paid by founders and employees who sell their shares.
However, because a significant portion of the consideration is in Intel stock, not all the proceeds will be realized immediately in cash.
One of Classiq’s private investors is Lip-Bu Tan, Intel’s current CEO, who has led the chipmaker’s turnaround over the past year and a half. Tan invested in Classiq personally before becoming CEO of the company now acquiring the startup. According to sources close to Classiq, he recused himself from discussions concerning the acquisition.
Other notable investors include NightDragon, a fund led by Dave DeWalt, who previously headed cybersecurity company McAfee.
Until recently, Classiq had been exploring a potential IPO on Wall Street, where several quantum computing companies have gone public over the past year. Most entered the public markets through mergers with special-purpose acquisition companies, or SPACs, and their subsequent share-price performance has been weak in recent months.
The only company to go public through a traditional IPO was Quantinuum, which debuted at a peak valuation of $15 billion. It has since lost 35% of its value and is currently valued at approximately $9.5 billion. IonQ, which went public through a SPAC merger in 2021, is now the most highly valued publicly traded quantum company, with a market capitalization of around $13 billion.

global-economics-f5b2c003e8.fulltext:
Written By Akriti AnandPublished26 Oct 2026, 01:59 PM IST
Unacademy founders Gaurav Munjal and Roman Saini are raising a ₹700-crore venture capital fund focused on artificial intelligence (AI) and deep technology startups, sources told the Economic Times in an exclusive interview.
The report comes less than two months after UpGrad acquired the education technology (edtech) company.
According to sources, the fund, named Longshot Capital, has secured commitments of about ₹300 crore and is targeting its first close in January 2027, following which it plans to start investing.
Who's running it: Roman Saini will lead the fund full-time, while Gaurav Munjal, who continues to head Unacademy, will be involved part-time, The Economic Times reported.
The plan: Longshot aims to back 25-28 seed and pre-Series A startups with initial cheques of 500,000-1.5 million, focusing on AI, manufacturing, space, defence and robotics.
The bigger picture: The two have made over 200 angel investments, deploying more than ₹25 crore. Their move follows other startup founders, including Snapdeal's Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, setting up investment funds.
UpGrad completed the acquisition of Unacademy for just over $200 million, about 94 per cent off its 2021 peak valuation, with co-founder and CEO Gaurav Munjal acknowledging the steep markdown in a post on LinkedIn, according to PTI.
Munjal wrote that the company became a unicorn (a privately held firm valued at more than USD 1 billion) six years ago. Unacademy had raised capital at its peak valuation but was ultimately sold for a fraction of that amount.
"Six years ago today, Unacademy became a unicorn. Today, Unacademy has closed its acquisition by UpGrad for just over USD 200 million. We raised at a peak, but sold at a fraction of that. I'm not going to dress these facts up," Munjal wrote on LinkedIn.
While Munjal did not quantify the exact markdown in his post, it may be recalled that back in 2021, Unacademy had raised USD 440 million (about ₹3,270.8 crore at that time) in funding from a clutch of investors including Temasek, General Atlantic, and Softbank Vision Fund, valuing the edtech major at USD 3.44 billion
The acquisition price of just over USD 200 million is, therefore, about 94 per cent lower than Unacademy's peak valuation.

Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata has challenged the resolution to reappoint N Chandrasekaran as chairman of Tata Sons, passed at a board meeting of the holding company of the Tata Group on September 17, according to a PTI report.
In a letter to Tata Sons company secretary Suprakash Mukhopadhyay on Monday, Noel challenged Chandrasekaran's reappointment for a further five-year term beyond February 2027, bringing differences within the conglomerate's board into the open.
Sources familiar with the development told PTI that Noel has termed the resolution void, citing several factors, including the notice and agenda for the meeting. He argued that the reappointment was taken up out of turn and was not included in the meeting's agenda, which was limited to a briefing by the nomination and remuneration committee, the sources said.
"The draft minutes [of the board meeting] are contested in material respects. The recording is the only neutral record of what transpired and there can be no legitimate reason to withhold it from a director who was present at the meeting and who has placed his objections on record," Tata wrote, according to a report by Businessline.
Noel, who heads Tata Trusts, which own about two-thirds of Tata Sons, had opposed Chandrasekaran's reappointment when it was put to a vote. However, Venu Srinivasan, the other Tata Trusts nominee director on the Tata Sons board, voted in favour of the reappointment along with the majority.
Other directors who supported Chandrasekaran's reappointment included Anita George, Harish Manwani and Saurabh Agarwal, according to PTI.
Noel has also argued that, under Tata Sons' Articles of Association, Tata Trusts' nominee directors must give their affirmative vote for a resolution to be passed.
In his letter, he sought an unedited video recording of the board meeting.
The dispute has also brought attention to reported business arrangements between TVS Motor Company and Hanno One Warehousing Pvt Ltd, which is linked to members of N Chandrasekaran's immediate family.
Citing media reports, Noel Tata has said that TVS Motor entered into agreements with Hanno One for warehousing and industrial park facilities. He has argued that the relationship should have been disclosed to the Tata Sons board before it considered Chandrasekaran's reappointment as executive chairman, according to multiple media reports.
Noel has also raised questions about whether Venu Srinivasan, chairman emeritus of TVS Motor and a Tata Sons board member who took part in the reappointment process, should have disclosed the relationship and abstained from the relevant discussions.

world-2d80e13770.headline: In their words: Global leaders congratulate Trump critic Lula on reelection in Brazil
world-2d80e13770.fulltext:
Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was reelected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of widening U.S. influence in Latin America. (AP video shot by Marko Alvarez and Maycron Abade)
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva celebrates with his running mate Geraldo Alckmin after winning a fourth term in the presidential runoff in , Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026.(AP Photo/Andre Penner)
Regional and world leaders congratulated Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva after he defeated challenger Flávio Bolsonaro to win an unprecedented fourth term.
Latin America’s left-leaning leaders were especially quick to react, but conservative presidents across the region also acknowledged Lula’s victory and emphasized the need for their countries to cooperate with Brazil on issues like fighting organized crime and reducing deforestation in the Amazon basin.
U.S. President Donald Trump had not acknowledged the election result by Monday afternoon and suggested, without providing evidence, that the vote count could have been “rigged” in Lula’s favor.
“Elections have to be indisputable and it looked very bad to me,” Trump told reporters before flying to Mississippi for a rally. He added, “I thought it had a very bad look, the way it was tabulated.”
In South America, the government of Argentina’s President Javier Milei was the only one that had not publicly acknowledged the result by Monday afternoon. After a Cabinet meeting Monday, Milei’s office issued a statement addressing several international developments, including the wars in Iran and Ukraine, but made no mention of the election outcome in neighboring Brazil. During the presidential campaign, the libertarian leader openly backed Bolsonaro and called Lula a “corrupt thief.”
Lula remains a revered figure on the region’s left, having governed Brazil from 2003 to 2010, when leftist leaders held power across much of Latin America. Over the past two years, however, Lula’s influence in South America has diminished, as most of Brazil’s neighbors elected right-wing governments aligned with the Trump administration.
Since returning to office in 2023, Lula has been a vocal Trump critic, challenging the administration on issues like trade tariffs and its support for Israel’s actions in the West Bank and Gaza.
On Monday, Lula was also congratulated by the leaders of the BRICS nations, an alliance of emerging economies that was designed to challenge Western dominance in international affairs. Brazil is a founding member of the alliance, which held its first summit in 2009, during Lula’s second term in office.
The leaders of major European nations also congratulated Lula, expressing their willingness to work with Brazil on issues like climate change.
Dear brother Lula, on behalf of the Cuban government and people, I congratulate you for this historic victory that ensures the continuity of the path of peace, sovereignty and social justice embarked upon by the Brazilian people under your leadership. Brazil can count on Cuba in the construction of the unity and integration of our Great Homeland, Latin America and the Caribbean.
President Lula and I have big, profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on something fundamental: Brazil and Colombia mutually need each other. We have a lot to do for the benefit of our people. Mutual respect, sovereignty and cooperation should define our relationship as well as the fight against narcoterrorism, illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon and the welfare of our people.
Chile and Brazil have a lot of shared future ahead, and we will continue working on an agenda that strengthens relations between our countries in economic integration and the fight against organized crime in the region.
Congratulations to Lula on this victory. Our region has common enemies, shared challenges and much to gain when we work together.
As we approach the bicentennial of our diplomatic relations, I reaffirm our willingness to strengthen our strategic alliance, integration, cooperation and the sustainable development of the Amazon that we share, for the benefit of both our peoples.
Bolivia and Brazil are neighboring and sister countries, united by a shared history and common challenges. We will continue working together to strengthen our relationship and generate more opportunities for our nations.
Congratulations, Lula, for your election as Brazil’s president. I salute the Brazilian people for this great democratic day. Paraguay and Brazil share a common agenda of integration and development. We will continue to work together for the benefit of our people.
Congratulations to the Brazilian people for exercising their right to vote, and for electing their new president in a democratic and peaceful process. I wish the greatest prosperity to the 212 million brothers and sisters who live in the largest country in Latin America.
Congratulations (...) to you, comrade President Lula, who in your seventh presidential election knew how to awaken your compatriots’ passions and their reason to win this battle.
A great victory for Lula! What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain. The comeback of global progressivism has just begun.
My heartfelt congratulations to Lula on your reelection. France and Brazil have much to build together. In the face of the great challenges of our time, let us strengthen our strategic partnership and bring to life the friendship between our two countries in service of a more just world.
Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil. Europe’s partnership with Brazil is thriving. We will remain by your side for the years to come. Together we will keep working closely for free and open trade. A rules-based global order. And strong ambitions for our climate.
Lula has stood up for Brazilian workers & democracy — and will continue to do so in the next four years.
For us in Ukraine, it is important that Brazil remains active in international affairs and continues to contribute to the effective protection of human rights, the rights of peoples, and the rights of states. We thank Brazil for its unwavering support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. We look forward to expanding our cooperation.
The election results fully reaffirmed your fellow citizens’ recognition of your outstanding leadership qualities and their support for your policies aimed at ensuring the country’s sustainable socioeconomic development and defending its sovereignty and legitimate interests on the world stage.
We will, of course, continue working closely together to expand our fruitful bilateral cooperation across all areas and our constructive engagement within the United Nations, BRICS, the G20 and other multilateral frameworks.
My sincerest congratulations to my dear friend, President Lula, on his remarkable victory in the reelection.
Together, we will continue to strengthen our cooperation in various sectors, promote the shared priorities of the global south, and work toward a more inclusive, equitable, and sustainable world.
China (...) expresses its congratulations. We are ready to work with Brazil to continue advancing the building of a China-Brazil community with a shared future.
This victory will echo beyond the shores of Brazil. It is a victory for the global south and progressive forces throughout the world. We affirm our commitment to continue strengthening bilateral relations between our two countries and working closely together in all multilateral fora to forge a just and better world order underpinned by solidarity and adherence to international law.

world-8e22bd67e6.headline: Anthropic files for potentially the biggest IPO ever as CEO warns of risk to humanity from AI
world-8e22bd67e6.fulltext:
The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the SpaceX initial public offering in June that raised a record $86 billion. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public in what is expected to be a pair of blockbuster stock debuts for the rival AI labs.
Dario Amodei, CEO and co-founder of Anthropic, attends the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Jan. 23, 2025. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber, File)
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for what could be the biggest initial public offering of stock ever, even as its top executive warns that advanced AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.
The filing sets up the San Francisco company for a Wall Street debut next month, potentially eclipsing the record $86 billion raised by SpaceX in its initial public offering in June. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public, setting the stage for a pair of blockbuster stock debuts by rival AI developers.
An IPO could give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion. The amount the company ultimately raises remains uncertain, as do its final valuation and offering price. But even at lower estimates, it would turn the five-year-old startup into one of the world’s most valuable companies, potentially adding billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela.
The 335-page filing showed Anthropic’s revenue is growing rapidly, reaching more than $16 billion in the first half of the year — 14 times its revenue from the same period last year. But like many other tech companies going public, the company behind the Claude chatbot has yet to turn a profit.
AP correspondent Bernard Condon reports details of Anthropic’s initial public offering are potentially frightening.
Despite the losses, Anthropic, valued earlier this year at $965 billion by private investors, is reportedly set to see that value rise to $1.5 trillion or possibly $2 trillion, although its final valuation has not been established. At $1.5 trillion, Anthropic would rank among the world’s most valuable public companies, alongside Tesla.
As for money raised, the offering could bring in as much as $100 billion, according to reports, surpassing the record set by SpaceX.
In a regulatory filing, Anthropic said it will list its stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol “ANT.”
In the filing, the company said it could use some of that money on acquiring other businesses and technology as well as investing in infrastructure to grow its business to take on rivals.
Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But they have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs of resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble.
The need for cash may explain why Anthropic is rushing to tap public markets this year, and not waiting until next year, as is OpenAI’s plan. Adding to the pressure is the possibility demand for AI shares could drop, or even collapse. Investors have become jittery about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.
David Hsu, a management professor at the University of Pennsylvania, said he sees the filing more as a move to diversify the company’s financial base.
“Obviously, they feel great, or at least good enough, on the safety aspects relative to OpenAI, and so that puts them in a position to really stay on track now to go public (first),” Hsu said.
In addition to helping plug any cash shortfall, the IPO will shower extraordinary wealth on Anthropic’s seven founders, including Amodei and his sister. The filing didn’t directly state their ownership stakes, but other figures disclosed suggest each will end up with 1.4% of the company, a windfall of as much as $28 billion a person should the company go public at the top expected value.
Dario, 43, and 39-year-old Daniela, who is Anthropic’s president, are already worth $15.5 billion each, according to Forbes, which ranks them as the 176th and 177th richest in the world.
Anthropic reported a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, although that included a one-time, $72.4 billion charge for an accounting adjustment related to financing agreements, according to the filing. In the same period a year ago, Anthropic lost $13 billion.
The document includes some unusual provisions, including granting those two and their five other co-founders 50.1% of shareholder votes through a special class of shares. Anthropic also has appointed independent, financially disinterested members of a so-called Long-Term Benefit Trust, holding power to appoint directors, that is designed to ensure the company doesn’t put financial interests ahead of public safety.
Another unusual feature of the filing is its long list of “risk factors,” a required disclosure for every public company but in this case one that runs nearly 100 pages — and makes for riveting reading.
Among the risks are the quotidian — the possibility it won’t be able to retain key staff or navigate regulatory roadblocks — and the horrific. The latter includes the prospect of “malicious actors” using AI models to build chemical weapons, authoritarian rulers turning to the technology to crack down on their citizens and the possibility that its AI models could go rogue and “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
Anthropic and other leading companies have touted the technology’s potential to cure diseases and speed economic growth. But it also threatens major disruptions to jobs by reducing the need for human labor.
A string of hacking incidents by rogue AI agents also has raised fears the technology will slip free of human control to carry out harmful, life-threatening tasks.
In September, Amodei said the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months.
He offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, noting that Anthropic is already undertaking part of this on its own. As for other steps, though, he said that would require coordination across the industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.
Anthropic has tried to set itself apart from other AI companies as the “good guys,” focusing on safety and responsible development as opposed to growing at all costs. Some of this sentiment stems from the company’s dispute with the U.S. government, which broke out in February when the Trump administration accused Anthropic of endangering national security and designated the company a supply chain risk.
Anthropic sued the Pentagon in March for what it called an “unlawful campaign of retaliation” over its refusal to allow unrestricted military use of its technology. The legal challenge intensified a dispute over how AI can be used in warfare and mass surveillance.
ChatGPT maker OpenAI made its own deal to work with the Pentagon hours after the government punished Anthropic for its stance. Anthropic also filed a separate and narrower case involving a different rule the Pentagon is using to try to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk.
A California judge ruled in Anthropic’s favor in the first case and a Washington, D.C. judge sided with the government in the second. Both sides are appealing the decisions.
Bernard Condon reported from New York. Associated Press writer Kaitlyn Huamani contributed from Los Angeles.
